ProphecySummary: In the garden God promised that the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent's head, even though his own heel would be struck. It is the first glimmer of the gospel — a descendant of Eve would undo the curse Satan had brought.
Fulfillment: In Jesus, born of a woman, Satan was decisively defeated at the cross and empty tomb, though Christ suffered in the victory. Paul and John both look back to this promise as fulfilled in Him, with its final outworking still to come at His return.
RelatedEvents: The Fall; The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Prophecy: Blessing to All Nations Through Abraham
ProphecySummary: God promised Abraham that through his offspring all families of the earth would be blessed. This was more than land and descendants — it pointed to a blessing that would reach the Gentile world.
Fulfillment: Paul identifies the offspring as Christ, through whom the blessing of Abraham and the gift of the Spirit have come to the nations. Every believer from every people group is living proof of this promise being kept.
RelatedEvents: The Call of Abraham; The Crucifixion; Pentecost

ProphecySummary: On Mount Moriah Abraham declared that God Himself would provide the lamb, and a ram was offered in Isaac's place. The place, the substitute, and the father's willingness all pointed beyond that day.
Fulfillment: Christians see the fulfilment on that same mountain ridge in Jerusalem, where God provided His own Son as the Lamb offered in our place. John's Gospel calls Jesus the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
RelatedEvents: The Binding of Isaac; The Crucifixion

Prophecy: The Scepter Will Not Depart from Judah
ProphecySummary: Jacob blessed Judah as a lion and promised that the scepter would not depart from him until the one to whom it belongs comes. Rulership, in other words, would run through Judah's line to a coming king who would receive the obedience of the nations.
Fulfillment: The promise narrowed through David, of Judah's tribe, and reached its fulfilment in Jesus, the Lion of the tribe of Judah. Revelation presents Him as that promised ruler whose kingdom gathers people from every nation.
RelatedEvents: Davidic Covenant; The Birth of Jesus

ProphecySummary: Hired to curse Israel, Balaam instead blessed them and saw a star and a scepter rise out of Jacob in the distant future. The vision pointed to a king who would triumph over Israel's enemies.
Fulfillment: Christians connect the star with the star of Bethlehem and the scepter with Jesus the King, born centuries later. His victory is not by the sword but by the cross, and it will be completed when He returns.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus

ProphecySummary: Moses promised that God would raise up a prophet like him from among Israel, to whose words the people must listen. For centuries Israel waited for this definitive spokesman of God.
Fulfillment: Peter and Stephen both identify Jesus as that prophet in Acts, greater than Moses because He is the Son over God's house. In Him God has spoken His final word, and listening to Him is life itself.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Commandments; The Sermon on the Mount

ProphecySummary: Through Nathan, God promised David a son whose kingdom and throne would be established forever. No merely human king could carry a promise that large, and Israel learned to hope for a greater Son of David.
Fulfillment: Gabriel announced the fulfilment to Mary: her son Jesus would receive the throne of His father David and reign forever. Peter preached at Pentecost that the risen Christ now sits on that throne.
RelatedEvents: Davidic Covenant; The Birth of Jesus; Pentecost

Prophecy: God's Anointed Son Rules the Nations
ProphecySummary: Psalm 2 declares that despite the nations raging, God has installed His King on Zion and given Him the nations as His inheritance. The Son is urged to be kissed — welcomed in glad submission.
Fulfillment: The New Testament applies this psalm to Jesus again and again: at His baptism, in His resurrection, and in His exaltation over every power. His present reign will be openly seen when He returns.
RelatedEvents: The Baptism of Jesus; The Resurrection

Prophecy: The Holy One Will Not See Decay
ProphecySummary: David confessed that God would not abandon his soul to the grave or let His Holy One see corruption. David himself died and decayed, so the words reached beyond him to someone greater.
Fulfillment: Peter and Paul both preach this as the resurrection of Jesus, whose body did not decay because God raised Him on the third day. It remains one of the clearest Old Testament anchors for Easter hope.
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection

ProphecySummary: Psalm 22 voices forsakenness, mocking crowds, pierced hands and feet, and soldiers dividing garments and casting lots. Written a thousand years before Christ — and before crucifixion was used in Israel — its detail is startling.
Fulfillment: Jesus cried its opening words from the cross, and the Gospels record its details fulfilled one by one, down to the lot cast for His clothing. The psalm ends in triumph, picturing the nations turning to the Lord.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion

ProphecySummary: Psalm 110 joins two offices Israel always kept apart: the promised King is also a priest forever, after the order of the mysterious Melchizedek. He rules from Zion and intercedes without end.
Fulfillment: Hebrews shows Jesus as that priest-king, not by Levitical descent but by the power of an indestructible life. Because He lives forever, He always intercedes for those who draw near to God through Him.
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; The Ascension

ProphecySummary: To a faithless king, Isaiah gave a sign: the virgin would conceive and bear a son called Immanuel, God with us. Offered in Ahaz's day, the promise carried a reach far beyond that crisis.
Fulfillment: Matthew declares the fulfilment in the conception of Jesus by the Holy Spirit and His birth to Mary. Immanuel is not just a name but the reality of the whole Gospel — God truly with us in Christ.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus

Prophecy: A Child Born, the Prince of Peace
ProphecySummary: In Galilee's darkness Isaiah saw light: a child born who would be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. His government and peace would have no end.
Fulfillment: Jesus was born into that same Galilee of the nations and began His ministry there, exactly where Isaiah pointed. His kingdom is already advancing, and its full peace awaits His return.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Sermon on the Mount

ProphecySummary: From the seemingly cut-down stump of Jesse, Isaiah promised a Branch on whom the Spirit would rest in fullness. He would judge with righteousness, defend the poor, and bring a peace so deep even creation is healed.
Fulfillment: Jesus, descended from Jesse through David and anointed by the Spirit at His baptism, fulfils the portrait. The wolf-and-lamb peace of Isaiah's vision is inaugurated in His kingdom and will be completed in the new creation.
RelatedEvents: The Baptism of Jesus; The Birth of Jesus

Prophecy: The Blind See and the Lame Leap
ProphecySummary: Isaiah promised a day when the eyes of the blind would be opened, the ears of the deaf unstopped, and the lame would leap like deer. It would be God's own coming to save His people.
Fulfillment: When John the Baptist asked if Jesus was the one, Jesus simply pointed to this prophecy happening: the blind see, the lame walk, and the poor have good news preached to them.
RelatedEvents: The Baptism of Jesus

ProphecySummary: Isaiah heard a voice crying in the wilderness to prepare the way of the Lord and make His paths straight. Comfort was coming to Jerusalem, and every valley would be lifted up.
Fulfillment: All four Gospels apply these words to John the Baptist, who prepared the way by preaching repentance in the wilderness. In Jesus, the glory of the Lord Isaiah promised was revealed to all flesh.
RelatedEvents: The Baptism of Jesus

Prophecy: The Servant Brings Justice to the Nations
ProphecySummary: Isaiah's first Servant Song presents God's chosen Servant, filled with the Spirit, bringing justice to the nations gently — not crying out or breaking a bruised reed. He would not grow faint until justice is established on earth.
Fulfillment: Matthew quotes this song over Jesus' quiet, compassionate ministry of healing and mercy. The hope of the nations rests on this gentle King whose justice will finally fill the whole earth.
RelatedEvents: The Baptism of Jesus

ProphecySummary: God told His Servant it was too small a thing to restore Israel alone; He would also be a light for the Gentiles, carrying salvation to the ends of the earth. Israel's Messiah was always meant for the world.
Fulfillment: Simeon praised the infant Jesus as that light to the Gentiles, and Paul and Barnabas later quoted the same words as the warrant for their mission. The worldwide church is this prophecy unfolding.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; Paul's Missionary Journeys

ProphecySummary: Isaiah 53 presents a Servant despised and rejected, pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, bearing the sin of many like a lamb led to slaughter. By His wounds, others are healed.
Fulfillment: The New Testament returns to this chapter constantly: Jesus bore our sins in silence, and Philip explained this very passage to the Ethiopian official, who believed and was baptized. It is the Old Testament's fullest portrait of the cross.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion

ProphecySummary: Isaiah announced one anointed by the Spirit to proclaim good news to the poor, liberty to captives, and the year of the Lord's favour. It is a Jubilee picture — debts cancelled and the brokenhearted bound up.
Fulfillment: In Nazareth Jesus read these words aloud and declared, Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing. His whole ministry of mercy, forgiveness, and release is this promise in action.
RelatedEvents: The Sermon on the Mount

Prophecy: New Heavens and a New Earth
ProphecySummary: Isaiah ends by promising that God will create new heavens and a new earth where former sorrows are remembered no more. Weeping gives way to gladness, and wolf and lamb feed together in peace.
Fulfillment: Peter and John take up Isaiah's promise for the world to come, when righteousness dwells and every tear is wiped away. Believers taste its firstfruits now in new creation through Christ, and await its fullness at His return.
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection

ProphecySummary: As Judah's kings failed, Jeremiah promised a righteous Branch from David who would reign wisely, do justice, and be called The Lord Our Righteousness. In His days Judah would be saved and Israel live in safety.
Fulfillment: Jesus, David's descendant, is that righteous King — and remarkably, He does not only rule righteously, He becomes our righteousness. Paul celebrates that in Christ we have the very righteousness Jeremiah named.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus

ProphecySummary: Jeremiah promised a new covenant unlike the one broken at Sinai: God's law written on hearts, sins forgiven and remembered no more, and every believer knowing the Lord. It was Israel's greatest hope for a healed relationship with God.
Fulfillment: At the Last Supper Jesus lifted the cup and called it the new covenant in His blood, and Hebrews declares the promise kept. Forgiveness and a transformed heart are now the birthright of everyone in Christ.
RelatedEvents: The Last Supper; The Crucifixion

Prophecy: God the Shepherd, David the King
ProphecySummary: Against Israel's false shepherds, Ezekiel promised that God Himself would search for His sheep, and would set over them one shepherd, His servant David. He would feed them, bind up the injured, and make a covenant of peace with them.
Fulfillment: Jesus calls Himself the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, gathering one flock under one shepherd. The promised gathering continues today and will be complete when the Chief Shepherd appears.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion

ProphecySummary: In a valley of very dry bones, Ezekiel prophesied and watched them come together, receive breath, and stand as a vast army. God explained it plainly: the whole house of Israel, cut off in exile, would be opened from its graves and brought home by His Spirit.
Fulfillment: The return from exile under Cyrus was its first fulfilment, and the Spirit giving new life in Christ is its deeper one. Many also look for a fuller national and spiritual restoration still to come, which is why this prophecy is best marked as begun but not finished.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile; Pentecost

ProphecySummary: Nebuchadnezzar dreamed of a great statue — gold, silver, bronze, iron, and iron mixed with clay — struck by a stone cut without hands, which became a mountain filling the earth. Daniel explained it as a succession of kingdoms, ending with a kingdom God Himself would set up forever.
Fulfillment: Historians commonly trace the metals through Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, and Rome — the very empire standing when Christ was born. In Jesus, God's everlasting kingdom has broken in, though its mountain-like fullness still lies ahead.
RelatedEvents: Daniel in the Lions' Den; The Birth of Jesus

Prophecy: The Son of Man Receives the Kingdom
ProphecySummary: Daniel saw one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days, receiving dominion, glory, and a kingdom that would never be destroyed. All peoples and languages would serve Him.
Fulfillment: Son of Man was Jesus' favourite title for Himself, and He quoted Daniel at His trial, to the fury of His judges. His ascension began the fulfilment; His visible return, when every eye sees Him, will complete it.
RelatedEvents: The Ascension; The Crucifixion

ProphecySummary: Gabriel gave Daniel a timetable of seventy sevens decreed for his people and city, to finish transgression, atone for iniquity, and anoint a most holy place. After sixty-nine sevens, an anointed one would be cut off, and the city and sanctuary would face destruction.
Fulfillment: Many evangelical readers calculate the weeks to the ministry and death of Christ, followed by Jerusalem's fall in AD 70, while others place the final week entirely in the future. Because faithful scholars differ on the details, this prophecy is honestly marked Debated, even though its central focus on the Messiah is widely affirmed.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

ProphecySummary: Daniel closes with the Old Testament's clearest resurrection promise: many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life and some to shame and everlasting contempt. The wise will shine like the stars forever.
Fulfillment: Jesus echoes Daniel's words when He speaks of the resurrection of life and of judgment, and Paul builds his hope on the same promise. It still awaits the day of Christ's return, when it will be fulfilled in full.
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection

Prophecy: Out of Egypt I Called My Son
ProphecySummary: Hosea looked back to the exodus: when Israel was a child God loved him, and out of Egypt He called His son. It is first a tender history lesson about Israel, not an obvious prediction.
Fulfillment: Matthew sees a deeper pattern fulfilled when the child Jesus, taken to Egypt to escape Herod, is called back out of Egypt just as Israel was. Jesus relives Israel's story — and succeeds where Israel failed.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Birth of Jesus

Prophecy: The Spirit Poured Out on All Flesh
ProphecySummary: Joel promised a day when God would pour out His Spirit on all flesh — sons and daughters, old and young, even servants — accompanied by wonders and the great Day of the Lord. Everyone who calls on the Lord's name would be saved.
Fulfillment: Peter stood up at Pentecost and declared, This is what was uttered through Joel, as the Spirit fell on all kinds of people. The cosmic signs and final Day still await completion, so Pentecost is the glorious beginning, not the whole fulfilment.
RelatedEvents: Pentecost

Prophecy: Restoration of the Booth of David
ProphecySummary: Amos ends with hope: God would raise up the fallen booth of David, repair its breaches, and restore the days of plenty. The restored people would possess the nations called by God's name and never again be uprooted.
Fulfillment: At the Jerusalem Council, James quoted this very text to show that Gentiles being gathered into Christ's church was David's tent being rebuilt. Its full picture of settled, fruitful restoration still awaits the kingdom's completion.
RelatedEvents: Jerusalem Council

ProphecySummary: Micah named tiny Bethlehem Ephrathah as the birthplace of a ruler whose coming forth is from ancient days, who would shepherd His people in the strength of the Lord. Bethlehem was David's town — a fitting, humble cradle for David's greater Son.
Fulfillment: When Herod asked where the Christ was to be born, the chief priests quoted Micah directly, and the Magi found Jesus in Bethlehem exactly as written. Matthew presents it as straightforward, deliberate fulfilment.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus

Prophecy: The King Comes on a Donkey
ProphecySummary: Zechariah called Jerusalem to rejoice: her King was coming, righteous and having salvation, yet humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt the foal of a donkey. He would speak peace to the nations and rule to the ends of the earth.
Fulfillment: Jesus deliberately arranged His entry into Jerusalem exactly this way on Palm Sunday, and both Matthew and John quote Zechariah to make sure we notice. The peace to the nations that Zechariah promised is still spreading through His church.
RelatedEvents: Triumphal Entry

ProphecySummary: Zechariah, acting out God's shepherd role, was paid thirty pieces of silver — the price of a slave — and threw the insulting sum to the potter in the house of the Lord. It pictured how cheaply God's shepherd would be valued.
Fulfillment: Judas agreed to betray Jesus for thirty pieces of silver, then in remorse threw the money into the temple, and it bought a potter's field. Matthew explicitly connects the painful details with what Zechariah (and Jeremiah's potter imagery) had spoken.
RelatedEvents: The Last Supper; The Crucifixion

ProphecySummary: Zechariah promised that God would pour out a spirit of grace on Jerusalem so that they would look on the one they had pierced and mourn for him as for an only son. Piercing, grief, and grace are bound together in a single piercing promise.
Fulfillment: John records that a soldier pierced Jesus' side and quotes Zechariah directly: They will look on him whom they have pierced. Revelation extends the looking to His return, when every eye will see Him and the mourning becomes worldwide.
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion

Prophecy: Strike the Shepherd, Scatter the Sheep
ProphecySummary: Zechariah heard God's sword awake against His shepherd, the man who stands next to Him: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered. Yet a refined remnant would survive the scattering and call on God's name.
Fulfillment: Jesus quoted this verse on the night of His arrest to explain why all His disciples would fall away and flee. They did scatter — and, as Zechariah also promised, they were gathered again after the resurrection.
RelatedEvents: Jesus Prays in Gethsemane; The Crucifixion

Prophecy: The Day of the Lord on the Mount of Olives
ProphecySummary: Zechariah's final vision sees the Lord coming with His holy ones, His feet standing on the Mount of Olives, which splits in two, and the Lord becoming King over all the earth. Living waters flow from Jerusalem, and there is no more curse.
Fulfillment: This still awaits fulfilment at Christ's return — fittingly, He ascended from the Mount of Olives and angels promised He would return the same way. Readers differ on how literally to take each detail, but its centre is clear: the Lord Himself will come and reign.
RelatedEvents: The Ascension

ProphecySummary: Malachi promised a messenger who would prepare the way before the Lord's sudden coming to His temple, like a refiner's fire purifying the sons of Levi. He closes the Old Testament by pointing to Elijah coming before the great Day of the Lord.
Fulfillment: Jesus identifies John the Baptist as this messenger and as Elijah who was to come, preparing hearts by repentance before Christ's appearing. A future, fuller coming before the final Day is also debated, but the primary fulfilment in John is Jesus' own verdict.
RelatedEvents: The Baptism of Jesus

Prophecy: The Glory of the Second Temple
ProphecySummary: To builders discouraged by the modest second temple, Haggai promised that its latter glory would be greater than the former glory of Solomon's temple, and that in this place God would give peace. The treasures of the nations would come in.
Fulfillment: Many Christians see the greater glory in the fact that Jesus Himself taught and was presented in that temple, while others look for a still-future glory. Because faithful readings differ, this is marked Debated — though no one disputes the promise ends in God's peace in that place.
RelatedEvents: Rebuilding of the Temple; The Birth of Jesus

ProphecySummary: On the Mount of Olives Jesus foretold the temple's destruction, wars, persecution, false prophets, and the gospel preached to all nations before the end. He also promised His own return in glory and warned His followers to stay awake and ready.
Fulfillment: The temple's fall in AD 70 fulfilled the first horizon of the prophecy with sobering precision, while the final return and judgment still lie ahead. How much belongs to each horizon is honestly debated, so this is marked Partially Fulfilled.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Triumphal Entry

Prophecy: The Second Coming and New Creation
ProphecySummary: Revelation unveils Jesus returning as King of kings on a white horse to judge and reign, followed by a new heaven and new earth where God dwells with His people. Every tear is wiped away, death and pain are no more, and the curse is lifted forever.
Fulfillment: This is the church's great future hope and has not yet been fulfilled — which is why Revelation ends with longing: Amen. Come, Lord Jesus. Its certainty anchors believers the way Hebrews 6:19 describes hope: firm and secure, like an anchor for the soul.
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection; The Ascension

ProphecySummary: In the church at Antioch, the prophet Agabus stood up and signified by the Spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world. The prophecy named a coming famine, not a local shortage, and it was given before the need arose. The disciples therefore determined to send relief to the brethren in Judaea, each according to his ability.
Fulfillment: Luke records that the famine came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar, matching the reign in which the great famine is known from history. The Antioch church sent its gift by Barnabas and Saul to the elders in Jerusalem, turning the warning into practical help. The prediction and its recorded outcome together mark it as fulfilled.
RelatedEvents: Famine under Claudius

ProphecySummary: At Caesarea the prophet Agabus took Paul's girdle, bound his own hands and feet, and said that so the Jews at Jerusalem would bind the man who owned the girdle and deliver him to the Gentiles. Paul himself had already said that the Holy Ghost witnessed in every city that bonds and afflictions awaited him. When friends begged him not to go up to Jerusalem, Paul answered that he was ready not only to be bound but also to die for the name of the Lord Jesus.
Fulfillment: At Jerusalem Paul was seized in the temple, bound, and delivered into Roman custody, exactly as Agabus had dramatised. He was then taken through a series of hearings and finally to Rome, where his bonds became the setting for his witness. The binding prophecy is therefore fulfilled in the arrest and imprisonment recorded in Acts.
RelatedEvents: Arrest of Paul

Prophecy: Ahijah: The Kingdom Torn from Solomon's Son
ProphecySummary: Ahijah the Shilonite met Jeroboam outside Jerusalem, tore his new cloak into twelve pieces, and gave Jeroboam ten, saying that the LORD would tear the kingdom out of Solomon's hand and give ten tribes to Jeroboam. One tribe would be left to Solomon's son for David's sake and for Jerusalem's sake, so that David would always have a lamp before the LORD there.
Fulfillment: When Rehoboam refused to lighten the people's burden, ten tribes rebelled and made Jeroboam king, while Judah and Benjamin stayed with Rehoboam at Jerusalem. The division lasted for the rest of the kingdom's history and was never healed, exactly as Ahijah had described it. The promise that David's lamp would remain in Jerusalem held alongside the judgment, and is part of why this entry does not duplicate the existing Eternal Throne entry.
RelatedPeople: Ahijah; Jeroboam; King Solomon; Rehoboam; David
RelatedEvents: The Kingdom Divides

ProphecySummary: Jeremiah asked why Milcom, the god of Ammon, possessed Gad's inheritance, and foretold that an alarm of war would be heard in Rabbah of the Ammonites, that it would become a desolate heap, and that its daughters would be burned with fire. Israel would then be heir to those who had been his heirs, and Ammon's king and princes would go into captivity. The oracle ends with a promise that God would bring again the captivity of Ammon in the latter days.
Fulfillment: Rabbah was conquered by Babylon, Ammon lost its independence, and the Ammonites as a distinct nation faded from history, with their territory absorbed by later powers. The desolation of Rabbah and the captivity of its leadership match the Babylonian conquest. The latter-days restoration strand has no clear historical fulfilment identified, so the entry is marked partially fulfilled.
RelatedEvents: Babylonian Conquest of Ammon

Prophecy: The Angel Assures Paul Before the Shipwreck
ProphecySummary: On Paul's voyage to Rome, after many days without sun or stars and with all hope of being saved taken away, an angel of God stood by Paul at night. The angel told him not to fear, for he must be brought before Caesar, and that God had given him all those sailing with him. Paul was assured that there would be no loss of any man's life, though the ship itself would be lost.
Fulfillment: The ship ran aground and broke apart, just as the angel had said the vessel would be lost. Yet all two hundred and seventy-six people aboard reached land safely, some on boards and some on broken pieces of the ship. The prediction was fulfilled in both halves, the loss of the ship and the preservation of every life.
RelatedEvents: Paul Shipwrecked on Malta

Prophecy: The Anointed King and His Bride
ProphecySummary: The psalm celebrates a king in majesty, girded with glory and honour, whose throne is for ever and ever and whose sceptre is a right sceptre. His bride, in gold of Ophir, is brought to him in joy, and the peoples are called to honour him. The song looks beyond any one royal wedding to a King whose reign and marriage are everlasting.
Fulfillment: Hebrews applies the words 'Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever' directly to the Son, identifying Christ as the anointed King of the psalm. The bridal picture is still unfolding in Scripture, reaching toward the marriage supper of the Lamb in Revelation. The entry is therefore partially fulfilled, with the King's identity settled in Christ and the wedding consummation still to come.
RelatedEvents: Marriage Supper of the Lamb

ProphecySummary: John told his readers that it was the last hour, and that just as they had heard an antichrist was coming, many antichrists had already come — and by this they would know it was the last hour. These antichrists went out from the church but were not truly of it, and their mark was denial of Jesus as the Christ and denial of the Father and the Son. The prophecy is therefore both a warning about a coming figure and a present sign: the spirit of antichrist was already at work through those who denied the incarnate Son.
Fulfillment: John states the sign as already present in his own day, with former members denying Christ and leaving the fellowship, and the same denial has recurred ever since. This entry is kept distinct from the man of lawlessness entry because John describes many present antichrists defined by doctrinal denial, rather than Paul's single future figure of lawlessness. Fulfillment is therefore partial and ongoing: begun in the first century and continuing wherever Christ is denied, with the final antichrist still awaited in the broader New Testament picture.
RelatedEvents: Day of the Lord

ProphecySummary: Paul foretold that in later times some would depart from the faith, giving heed to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, including forbidding marriage and commanding abstinence from foods God created to be received with thanksgiving. In the last days, he said, perilous times would come, marked by lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastfulness, disobedience, unthankfulness, lack of self-control, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, and a form of godliness that denies its power. These are presented as a widespread moral and doctrinal falling away, not a single event or single figure, which is why the two pastoral passages are grouped here as one prophecy.
Fulfillment: The New Testament itself presents this falling away as already beginning, with false teaching and ungodly conduct appearing in the early churches, and church history since has repeatedly shown the same pattern of doctrinal departure and moral decline. Because the passages describe a recurring condition of the last days rather than one datable event, fulfillment is best understood as partially fulfilled and ongoing, culminating in the final rebellion described in 2 Thessalonians 2. It is kept distinct from the man of lawlessness entry, which concerns a specific revealed figure rather than this general departure.
RelatedEvents: Day of the Lord

ProphecySummary: Isaiah foretold that Assyria, the rod of God's anger, would overreach itself and be broken, and that Jerusalem would not fall to it. The Assyrian king's boasts would end in defeat, his army would be shattered, and the yoke on God's people would be lifted. The same deliverance is promised again in the oracles against trusting Egypt's horses and chariots instead of the LORD.
Fulfillment: In 701 BC Sennacherib's army besieged Jerusalem but withdrew after a devastating loss in its camp, as recorded in 2 Kings 19:35 and Isaiah 37:36, and Jerusalem survived. Assyria's power then waned, and Nineveh itself fell to Babylon and Media in 612 BC. The prediction of Assyria broken and Jerusalem spared was therefore fulfilled in history.
KeyPassages: Isaiah 10:5-19; Isaiah 10:24-34; Isaiah 14:24-27; Isaiah 30:27-33; Isaiah 31:4-9; Isaiah 36:1-22; Isaiah 37:1-38; 2 Kings 19:35
RelatedPeople: Isaiah; King Hezekiah; Sennacherib, King of Assyria; Rabshakeh
RelatedEvents: Hezekiah and Sennacherib's Invasion; Fall of Nineveh

ProphecySummary: Jeremiah's long oracle against Babylon, written and sent to Babylon in Zedekiah's fourth year, foretold that Babylon would be taken, its idols Bel and Merodach confounded and broken, and its mighty men would cease fighting. The land would be made desolate, its treasures spoiled, and the broad walls of Babylon utterly broken down. This entry covers the judgment strand of Jeremiah 50-51; the return strand of those chapters is grouped separately in the Return from Exile entry.
Fulfillment: Babylon fell to Cyrus in 539 BC without a great battle for its walls, its empire ended, its idols proved powerless, and its great city declined over the following centuries until its site was desolate. The judgment foretold while Babylon was still at the height of its power was therefore fulfilled. It is distinct from Isaiah's Babylon oracle, which was spoken more than a century earlier.
RelatedPeople: Jeremiah; Cyrus the Great; Belshazzar; Seraiah
RelatedEvents: Fall of Babylon

ProphecySummary: Long before Babylon was the dominant power, Isaiah foretold its fall: its golden city would be brought low, its idols Bel and Nebo would stoop and be carried away, and the proud oppressor would be humbled. The burden against Babylon, the night vision of a watchman, and the later taunt against Babylon's sorceries and pride all speak of the same downfall. This entry folds Isaiah 47-48 into the Babylon oracle rather than duplicating it.
Fulfillment: Babylon fell to Cyrus the Persian in 539 BC, its empire ended, and its great city declined until its site was desolate, as the later history of the region shows. The idols that could not save Babylon were indeed carried off as spoil, and the city never regained its imperial glory. The prediction was therefore fulfilled, strikingly, more than a century and a half after Isaiah spoke.
KeyPassages: Isaiah 13:1-22; Isaiah 14:3-23; Isaiah 21:1-10; Isaiah 46:1-2; Isaiah 47:1-15; Isaiah 48:14-20
RelatedEvents: Fall of Babylon; Return from Exile

ProphecySummary: Hired by Balak to curse Israel, Balaam found he could only bless them, and his oracles went on to foretell the fates of the surrounding nations. Beyond the star out of Jacob, which is already covered by an existing entry, Balaam said that Moab and Edom would be dispossessed, Amalek would perish, the Kenites would be carried away captive, and ships from Kittim would afflict Asshur and Eber.
Fulfillment: Moab was subdued under David and Edom was made subject to Israel, while Amalek was struck down in Saul's and David's campaigns until the people faded from history. The Kenite captivity and the Kittim-Asshur sayings are harder to pin to single dated events, and scholars debate whether they point to Assyrian, Greek, or Roman powers. This entry is therefore marked Partially Fulfilled, covering the nation oracles other than the star, which remains in its own existing entry.
RelatedPeople: Balaam; Balak; Moses; David; King Saul
RelatedEvents: Wilderness Wanderings; David's Conquests

ProphecySummary: When Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, despaired over the sorrows added to his pain, the LORD told him not to seek great things for himself, for evil would be brought upon all flesh, but that his life would be given to him for a prey in every place he went. It is a personal prophecy to a named individual, spoken in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, and it is included here as a borderline entry on the same ground as the Rechabites and Ebed-Melech promises.
Fulfillment: Baruch survived the fall of Jerusalem, the turmoil that followed, and the flight into Egypt with the remnant, living through dangers that claimed many around him. His life was indeed preserved wherever he went, as the promise said. The prophecy was therefore fulfilled in his survival through the exile years.
RelatedPeople: Jeremiah; Baruch; Jehoiakim, King of Judah
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Flight to Egypt

Prophecy: The Battle Belongs to the LORD
ProphecySummary: When a vast army of Moabites, Ammonites, and Meunites came against Jehoshaphat, the Spirit of the LORD came on Jahaziel the Levite, who told the king and all Judah not to be afraid or dismayed, for the battle was not theirs but God's. They would not need to fight in this battle at all, but were to stand still and see the salvation of the LORD, going out against the enemy the next morning with the LORD with them.
Fulfillment: The next morning, as Judah's singers went out praising the LORD, the LORD set ambushes against the invading armies and they destroyed one another, so that when Judah reached the watchtower they saw only dead bodies and no one had escaped. Judah spent three days gathering the spoil, and the surrounding kingdoms feared God after hearing what He had done. This prophecy survives only in Chronicles, with no Kings parallel, and is therefore a genuinely new Chronicles item.
RelatedEvents: Jehoshaphat's Victory over Moab and Ammon

Prophecy: The Beasts from Sea and Land
ProphecySummary: John saw a beast rise from the sea with ten horns and seven heads, given authority by the dragon, blaspheming God and making war with the saints for forty-two months, and the whole earth wondered after it. A second beast rose from the land with two horns like a lamb but speaking like a dragon, performing great signs, making fire come down from heaven, and causing an image of the first beast to be made and worshipped, with death for all who would not worship it. This second beast caused all, small and great, rich and poor, free and bond, to receive a mark on the right hand or forehead, so that no one could buy or sell without the mark, the name of the beast, or the number of his name, 666. Those who worship the beast and receive its mark will drink of the wine of God's wrath and be tormented, while the saints are called to endurance and faith.
Fulfillment: The beasts' identities are debated — empire and false prophet, a future world ruler and his prophet, or recurring persecuting powers — and the mark's exact form is likewise debated, with buying and selling pointing to economic coercion for loyalty to the beast. The mark is folded into this entry rather than given its own, because Revelation presents it as the second beast's enforcement mechanism, not a separate prophecy. No specific historical ruler is named here, since the text does not name one.
RelatedEvents: Great Tribulation; Day of the Lord

ProphecySummary: David lamented that his own familiar friend, in whom he trusted and who ate of his bread, had lifted up his heel against him. Jesus applied that verse to His own circle, saying that one who ate bread with Him would betray Him. At the Last Supper He told the disciples plainly that one of them would betray Him, and Judas went out to do it.
Fulfillment: Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve who shared bread with Jesus, betrayed Him to the chief priests and identified Him with a kiss. The betrayal led directly to Jesus's arrest, trial, and crucifixion, exactly as the passion narrative records. This single entry covers both the psalm and the Gospel predictions, so the betrayal is not counted twice.
RelatedEvents: Last Supper; Arrest of Jesus Christ

ProphecySummary: Before Israel entered the land, Moses set before them blessing for obedience and curses for disobedience in full detail: a fruitful land and victory if they kept the covenant, and siege, scattering among all peoples, and a trembling heart if they turned away. Yet Moses also promised that when they were in exile and returned to the LORD with all their heart, God would gather them again, circumcise their hearts, and bring them back into the land.
Fulfillment: Israel's history followed the pattern Moses laid out: the northern kingdom fell to Assyria and Judah was carried to Babylon, with the temple destroyed and the people scattered. Under Cyrus the exiles were allowed to return and rebuild, as Ezra records, which fulfilled the return in its first, historical sense. Because the prophets also speak of a fuller gathering that Christians and Jews understand differently, this entry is marked Partially Fulfilled, with the exile and the return under Cyrus as the firmly historical core.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Samaria; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Return from Exile

Prophecy: The Chaldeans Raised Up and Judged
ProphecySummary: When Habakkuk questioned how God could tolerate Judah's injustice, God answered that He was raising up the Chaldeans, a bitter and hasty nation, to march through the breadth of the land and possess dwellings not their own. Habakkuk then questioned how a holy God could use a more wicked nation, and God answered again with five woes on the proud plunderer: woe to him who builds by blood, covets evil gain, and makes neighbours drunk with violence. The same passage promises that the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.
Fulfillment: The Chaldeans, that is the Neo-Babylonians under Nebuchadnezzar, did conquer Judah, destroy Jerusalem in 586 BC, and carry its people into exile, fulfilling the raising up. Babylon itself then fell to the Medes and Persians in 539 BC, fulfilling the woes on the plunderer in the broad sweep of history, even though the five woes are poetic and not each tied to a single dated battle. The knowledge of God's glory filling the earth is still unfolding, so the entry is partly fulfilled.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Fall of Babylon

Prophecy: A Child Named Josiah Shall Be Born
ProphecySummary: While Jeroboam stood burning incense at the altar he had built at Bethel, a man of God from Judah cried out against the altar, saying that a child would be born to the house of David named Josiah. That child, the prophecy said, would sacrifice the priests of the high places upon that very altar and burn men's bones upon it, and the altar itself would be torn down as a sign.
Fulfillment: About three centuries later, King Josiah of Judah came to Bethel, tore down the altar and the high place, burned the high place, and sacrificed the priests of the high places on the altar, fulfilling the word by name. The narrator of Kings pauses to note that Josiah spared only the tomb of the man of God who had spoken the prophecy. Naming a king centuries before his birth makes this one of the most specific predictions in the historical books.
RelatedEvents: Josiah's Reforms

Prophecy: Coniah's Line Cut Off from the Throne
ProphecySummary: Jeremiah foretold that Coniah, also called Jeconiah, king of Judah, would be cast out with his mother into a land where he was not born, and would die there, never to return. God swore that no man of his seed would prosper sitting upon the throne of David or ruling any more in Judah, and that Coniah would be written as childless in the sense of having no royal heir. It is a prophecy about a named king's dynasty, distinct from the promise of a righteous Branch in the same book.
Fulfillment: Jeconiah was carried to Babylon in 597 BC, lived out his life in exile, and never returned to rule, while no descendant of his sat on the throne of David in Judah after him. Matthew's genealogy still traces Jesus' legal line through Jeconiah, which has led interpreters to distinguish the royal succession in Judah from the messianic line, but the throne prediction itself held. The prophecy was therefore fulfilled in the end of Jeconiah's royal line.
RelatedEvents: Exile of Jeconiah; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Prophecy: The Curse and Wickedness Removed from the Land
ProphecySummary: Zechariah saw a flying scroll, twenty cubits by ten, carrying a curse that would enter the house of the thief and of him who swears falsely, and consume it with its timber and stones. He then saw wickedness as a woman shut in a basket with a lead cover, carried by two winged women to the land of Shinar, where a house would be built for her. Finally four chariots, the four spirits of heaven, went out from between mountains of brass to patrol the earth and bring quiet to God's Spirit in the north country.
Fulfillment: The visions promised a purged land for the restored community, and the post-exilic community did turn from the idolatry and covenant breaking that had caused exile, so a moral cleansing began in the return. Theft, false oath, and idolatry were not permanently removed from Israel or from the world, and Christians read the final removal of wickedness as awaiting Christ's judgment and the new creation. The entry is therefore partly fulfilled: the cleansing of the returned community began, while the complete removal of wickedness remains future.
RelatedEvents: Return from Exile; Rebuilding of the Temple

Prophecy: The Curse on Whoever Rebuilds Jericho
ProphecySummary: After Jericho fell, Joshua pronounced a solemn curse: whoever rose up to rebuild the city would lay its foundation at the cost of his firstborn son and set up its gates at the cost of his youngest son. The curse was spoken over a city devoted to destruction, and it stood as a warning for generations after the conquest.
Fulfillment: Centuries later, in the days of King Ahab, Hiel of Bethel rebuilt Jericho, and 1 Kings records that he laid its foundation with the loss of his firstborn Abiram and set up its gates with the loss of his youngest Segub, according to the word of the LORD by Joshua. The long gap between curse and fulfilment is itself part of the point: the word waited until someone dared to defy it.
RelatedPeople: Joshua; Hiel the Bethelite; King Ahab; Abiram; Segub
RelatedEvents: The Walls of Jericho

ProphecySummary: Isaiah addressed the land beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, whose ambassadors travelled by swift vessels of reeds, and foretold that a people tall and smooth, feared far and near, would be brought as a present to the LORD of hosts at Mount Zion. The oracle pictures distant Cush acknowledging the God of Israel at Jerusalem. Its exact historical referent is not named in the text, and this entry does not invent one.
Fulfillment: No single clear historical event is identified in Scripture as the fulfilment of this tribute, and interpreters differ on whether it points to a past embassy, to the Ethiopian eunuch's worship at Jerusalem, or to a still-future gathering of the nations at Zion. Because the referent and timing are genuinely debated, this entry is marked Debated rather than claimed as fulfilled or future with certainty. The text's promise of tribute to Zion remains, with its fulfilment left open rather than forced.
RelatedEvents: The Nations Come to Zion

ProphecySummary: Isaiah named Cyrus, king of Persia, more than a century before he was born, calling him God's anointed and shepherd, who would say to Jerusalem that it shall be built and to the temple that its foundation shall be laid. The LORD promised to go before Cyrus, break gates of brass, and give him the treasures of darkness, so that the exiles could return and rebuild. Cyrus is called God's anointed not as a messiah, but as an instrument chosen for liberation.
Fulfillment: Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BC and in 538 BC issued the decree allowing the Jews to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple, as recorded in Ezra 1 and 2 Chronicles 36:22-23. The naming of Cyrus in advance, the fall of Babylon, and the return and rebuilding all came to pass. This is one of the most precisely fulfilled predictions in Isaiah.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Babylon; Return from Exile; Rebuilding of the Temple

Prophecy: Damascus Ceases to Be a City
ProphecySummary: Isaiah foretold that Damascus would be taken away from being a city and become a ruinous heap, and that the fortress of Ephraim and the kingdom of Damascus would fail together. The glory of Jacob would be made thin in the same judgment, as Israel's northern kingdom shared Syria's fate. It is a prophecy of the end of Damascus as an Aramean capital and of Ephraim as a kingdom.
Fulfillment: Damascus was conquered by Assyria under Tiglath-Pileser III in 732 BC, its king was killed, and Aram ceased to be an independent power, while Ephraim fell to Assyria in 722 BC. Damascus as a place was later inhabited again, so the prophecy is best read as fulfilled in the end of its kingdom and capital status, not in permanent uninhabitation. It is therefore marked as partially fulfilled, with its political sense fulfilled in full.
RelatedPeople: Isaiah; Rezin; Pekah, King of Israel
RelatedEvents: Assyrian Conquest of Damascus; Fall of Samaria

ProphecySummary: Jeremiah foretold that Hamath and Arpad would be confounded by evil tidings, that Damascus would grow feeble and turn to flee, and that anguish and sorrows would take hold of her as a woman in travail. Fire would be kindled in the wall of Damascus and would consume the palaces of Benhadad. It is a short, distinct oracle against Damascus, separate from Isaiah's earlier Damascus oracle.
Fulfillment: Damascus was conquered by Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar, its power as a regional capital was broken, and its palaces and walls suffered the fire of conquest. The city was later inhabited again under later empires, so the prophecy is fulfilled in the breaking of its kingdom power, not in permanent uninhabitation. It is therefore marked partially fulfilled, with its political judgment fulfilled in full.
RelatedEvents: Babylonian Conquest of Damascus

Prophecy: The Day of the LORD on Judah
ProphecySummary: Zephaniah, speaking in the days of King Josiah, announced a Day of the LORD that would sweep away man and beast from the land and punish Jerusalem's idolaters. He pictured a day of wrath, trouble, distress, wasteness, desolation, darkness, and gloominess, with a trumpet against fenced cities and high towers. The proud who say the LORD will neither do good nor evil, and those clothed in strange apparel and leaping on thresholds in pagan ritual, would find their wealth plundered and their houses desolate.
Fulfillment: The near fulfillment came when Babylon besieged and destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC, ending the monarchy and temple worship Zephaniah had condemned, after Josiah's reforms had only delayed judgment. Zephaniah's language also reaches beyond 586 BC, using cosmic and universal terms that Christian tradition reads as pointing to a final Day of the LORD not yet arrived. The entry is therefore partly fulfilled: the historical Day on Judah came, while the ultimate Day remains future.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Day of the LORD; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Prophecy: Deborah: Sisera by a Woman's Hand
ProphecySummary: When Barak refused to go into battle without her, Deborah the prophetess told him that the LORD would sell Sisera into the hand of a woman, and that the honour of the victory would not be his. The word was spoken before the battle by the Kishon, where Sisera's nine hundred iron chariots were expected to decide the day.
Fulfillment: The LORD routed Sisera's army, Sisera fled on foot, and Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, drove a tent peg through his temple while he slept in her tent. Deborah and Barak's song afterwards blessed Jael above women in the tent, naming her as the one by whose hand the enemy commander fell. This is flagged as a borderline personal prediction, included because it decided a national battle and reversed the expected glory of war, as Scripture itself stresses.
RelatedEvents: Deborah and Barak Defeat Sisera

ProphecySummary: While Ben-hadad besieged Samaria and famine had driven food prices to unthinkable heights, Elisha announced that by tomorrow about that time a measure of fine flour and two measures of barley would each sell for a shekel at the gate of Samaria. A royal officer scoffed that even if the LORD made windows in heaven this could not happen, and Elisha told him he would see it with his eyes but not eat of it.
Fulfillment: That night the LORD made the Syrian army hear the sound of chariots and horses, and they fled, leaving their camp behind, so that the starving city plundered it and food prices fell to exactly what Elisha had said. The scoffing officer was trampled to death in the gate as the hungry crowd rushed out, seeing the plenty but not eating of it. The precision of price, place, and time makes this one of the most exactly dated predictions in Kings.
RelatedPeople: Elisha; Jehoram, King of Israel; Ben-hadad
RelatedEvents: Siege of Samaria

Prophecy: Delivered to Shishak, Yet Not Destroyed
ProphecySummary: After Rehoboam abandoned the law of the LORD, the prophet Shemaiah told him and the princes gathered at Jerusalem that because they had forsaken God, God had left them in the hand of Shishak king of Egypt. When they humbled themselves, a second word came: God would not destroy them but would grant them some deliverance, though they would become Shishak's servants so they might learn the difference between serving God and serving the kings of other lands.
Fulfillment: Shishak came up against Jerusalem in Rehoboam's fifth year with a great army and took the treasures of the house of the LORD and the king's house, including the gold shields Solomon had made. Jerusalem itself was not destroyed, Rehoboam humbled himself, and the wrath was turned away, though Judah remained weakened and tributary. This prophecy survives only in Chronicles, not in the parallel Kings account, and is therefore a genuinely new Chronicles item rather than a duplicate.
RelatedPeople: Shemaiah; Rehoboam; Shishak, King of Egypt; King Solomon
RelatedEvents: Shishak's Invasion of Judah

ProphecySummary: Ezekiel announced that Egypt would become desolate from Migdol to Syene, its people scattered among the nations for forty years, and that it would never again rule over other nations. Nebuchadnezzar would be given Egypt as wages for his long siege of Tyre, and Pharaoh's power would be broken. The oracles picture Egypt's pride, its allies, and its great river-god claims all brought low.
Fulfillment: Nebuchadnezzar campaigned against Egypt in 568 BC, and Egypt never again became an empire ruling other nations, passing instead under Persian, Greek, and Roman rule. Scholars debate the forty-year desolation, since no clear forty-year period of total emptiness is documented, so this entry is marked Partially Fulfilled. The lasting loss of imperial dominance is clear, while the precise desolation period remains debated.
RelatedEvents: Babylonian Campaign Against Egypt

ProphecySummary: The burden of Dumah is brief and haunting: one calls to the watchman out of Seir, asking what of the night, and the watchman answers that the morning comes, and also the night. It is a word to Edom's region of Dumah, holding out a morning that is still shadowed by night, and an invitation to return and enquire. The text names no dated invasion, and this entry does not supply one.
Fulfillment: No passage of Scripture or securely dated history identifies a single fulfilment for Dumah's night watch, and interpreters differ on whether it points to an Assyrian or Babylonian threat to Edom, to a longer night of judgment, or to a deliberately open-ended watchman's riddle. Because the referent is genuinely debated, this entry is marked Debated rather than tied to an invented campaign. It is included because it is a distinct burden against a named place, not a general saying.
RelatedEvents: Oracles Against the Nations

Prophecy: Judgment of the Earth and Death Swallowed Up
ProphecySummary: Isaiah looked beyond any single nation to a day when the LORD would lay the earth waste, scatter its inhabitants, and punish the host of the high ones and the kings of the earth. On Mount Zion he would make a feast for all peoples, swallow up death in victory, and wipe away tears from all faces, and the dead would live and rise. The same section promises Leviathan's defeat and Israel's regathering, a song of trust in a strong city, and a vineyard kept by the LORD.
Fulfillment: The swallowing up of death is claimed by the New Testament in the resurrection of Christ and is applied to the final resurrection, as in 1 Corinthians 15:54, while the universal judgment and the feast for all peoples have not yet been seen in full. The prophecy therefore stands partially fulfilled: death's defeat has begun in Christ, and its completion awaits the last day. It is distinct from the Daniel resurrection entry, which does not cite Isaiah 25.
RelatedEvents: The Last Judgment; The Resurrection; The Feast on Mount Zion

ProphecySummary: After Ebed-Melech the Ethiopian rescued Jeremiah from the cistern, the word of the LORD came to him promising that he would not be given into the hand of the men he feared, and that he would not fall by the sword when Jerusalem fell. His life would be given to him as a prey, because he had put his trust in the LORD. It is a personal promise of deliverance in the very siege that destroyed the city.
Fulfillment: When Jerusalem fell, Ebed-Melech was spared, as the promise said, while the city's princes and many others perished or were carried away. His deliverance is recorded in the context of the fall itself, and his trust in God is given as its reason. The prophecy was therefore fulfilled in his survival of the siege.
RelatedPeople: Jeremiah; Ebed-Melech; Zedekiah, King of Judah
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Jeremiah in the Cistern

ProphecySummary: Jeremiah foretold that Edom's wisdom would fail, that its people would be made small among the heathen and despised among men, and that its pride had deceived it. Bozrah would become a desolation, a reproach, and a curse, and Edom would become like Sodom and Gomorrah, with no man dwelling there. It is Jeremiah's own Edom oracle, distinct from Isaiah's Edom and day-of-vengeance entry, though it speaks of the same nation's fall.
Fulfillment: Edom was overrun by Babylon and later displaced by the Nabataeans, Bozrah and the Edomite territory were left desolate, and the Edomites as a nation disappeared, surviving only as Idumeans absorbed into later history. The desolation of Bozrah and the end of Edom as a people match the oracle. The prophecy was therefore fulfilled in Edom's disappearance as a nation.
RelatedEvents: Babylonian Conquest of Edom; Nabataean Displacement of Edom

Prophecy: Edom's Desolation and the Day of Vengeance
ProphecySummary: Isaiah foretold a sword bathed in heaven that would come down upon Edom, whose land would become burning pitch and a wilderness where no one passes through, inhabited by wild creatures. In the companion vision, one comes from Edom with garments stained red from Bozrah, having trodden the winepress alone in the day of vengeance and the year of his redeemed. The two passages are grouped here as one prediction, since they speak of the same judgment on Edom.
Fulfillment: Edom was overrun and displaced, its territory taken over by the Nabataeans, and the Edomites as a nation disappeared, with their land left desolate as the oracle pictures. The winepress figure of the day of vengeance is also read in the New Testament tradition as pointing to a final day of judgment not yet seen in full. The prophecy is therefore partially fulfilled: Edom's historical desolation has happened, and its final day remains future.
RelatedEvents: Judgment on Edom; The Day of Vengeance

ProphecySummary: Obadiah, the shortest book in the Old Testament, pronounced total judgment on Edom, descended from Esau, for standing aloof and then joining in the plunder when Jerusalem fell. Edom had gloated over Judah's calamity, blocked fugitives at the crossroads, and handed survivors to the enemy, breaking the bond of brotherhood. God promised that Edom's pride in its rocky strongholds would be brought down, its wise men and warriors destroyed, and no survivor left of the house of Esau, while Mount Zion would be holy and the kingdom would be the LORD's.
Fulfillment: Edom was struck by Babylon in the sixth century BC, then displaced from its homeland by the Nabataeans, surviving only as Idumea to the west before being absorbed under the Hasmoneans and disappearing as a distinct people after the first century AD. The final part of the oracle, the possession of Edom's land and the kingdom belonging to the LORD, is read in Christian tradition as completed in Christ's kingdom and awaiting its final consummation. The national doom of Edom is therefore fulfilled, with its kingdom consummation still future.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
Places: Edom; Seir; Bozrah; Teman; Jerusalem; Mount Zion; Petra

ProphecySummary: Jeremiah foretold Egypt's defeat at Carchemish, where Pharaoh Necho's army would be broken by Nebuchadnezzar, and a later invasion in which Nebuchadnezzar would strike the land of Egypt, set fire to its temples, and carry off its gods. Pharaoh Hophra would be given into the hand of his enemies, as Zedekiah had been given to Nebuchadnezzar. The oracle is distinct from Isaiah's Egypt oracle and from Jeremiah 44's warning to the remnant in Egypt, which is folded into this entry's background rather than duplicated.
Fulfillment: Egypt was defeated at Carchemish in 605 BC, ending its imperial ambitions in the Levant, and Nebuchadnezzar invaded Egypt in 568 BC, in the reign of Pharaoh Amasis after Hophra's fall. Egypt never regained its former imperial power, though it continued as a nation, so the judgment is marked fulfilled in its defeat and humbling. The later promise of Egypt's restoration after forty years, in Ezekiel rather than Jeremiah, is not claimed here.
RelatedPeople: Jeremiah; Pharaoh Necho; Hophra; King Nebuchadnezzar
RelatedEvents: Battle of Carchemish; Babylonian Invasion of Egypt

ProphecySummary: Isaiah foretold that the LORD would ride upon a swift cloud into Egypt, its idols would be moved, its spirit would fail, and Egyptians would fight against each other, city against city and kingdom against kingdom. Its wise counsellors would be confounded, the Nile's waters would fail, and Egypt would be given into the hand of a cruel lord. Yet the oracle also promises that Egypt will one day know the LORD and be healed, with an altar to the LORD in Egypt.
Fulfillment: Egypt was humbled by Assyrian invasion under Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal, and later by Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar, with internal strife and loss of imperial power matching the oracle's picture. The sign-act of Isaiah walking barefoot for three years pointed to Egypt and Ethiopia led away captive by Assyria, which history confirms. The final healing and worship strand of the oracle has not yet been seen in full, so the prophecy is partially fulfilled.
RelatedEvents: Assyrian Invasion of Egypt; Babylonian Invasion of Egypt

ProphecySummary: Jeremiah foretold that the LORD would break the bow of Elam, the chief of its might, bring the four winds against it, and scatter its people toward all winds until none were left to whom Elam's outcasts would not come. Its king and princes would be dismayed, yet the oracle ends with a promise that in the latter days God would bring again the captivity of Elam. It is the only Elam oracle in the prophets, and it holds judgment and restoration together.
Fulfillment: Elam was broken by Assyria and then absorbed into the Persian empire, its capital Susa becoming a Persian centre, and the Elamites as an independent power disappeared. The scattering of Elam matches that absorption into the empires that followed. The latter-days restoration strand has no clear historical fulfilment identified, so the entry is marked partially fulfilled.
RelatedEvents: Assyrian Conquest of Elam; Rise of Persia

ProphecySummary: When Joseph brought his two sons to Jacob for blessing, Joseph placed Manasseh, the firstborn, at Jacob's right hand and Ephraim at his left, but Jacob deliberately crossed his hands and put his right hand on Ephraim's head. Joseph objected, yet Jacob insisted that Manasseh would also become a people and be great, but that his younger brother Ephraim would be greater, and his offspring would become a multitude of nations.
Fulfillment: Ephraim became the dominant northern tribe: Joshua, who led Israel into the land, was an Ephraimite, and the first capital of the northern kingdom stood at Shechem in Ephraim's hill country. The name Ephraim later came to stand for the northern kingdom as a whole, just as Jacob's word had placed the younger brother first. This entry is a borderline blessing-or-prophecy case, included because Jacob's crossed hands were a deliberate, explicit prediction of relative greatness, not a general good wish.
RelatedPeople: Jacob; Joseph; Ephraim; Manasseh; Joshua; Jeroboam
RelatedEvents: Conquest of Canaan; The Kingdom Divides

ProphecySummary: John saw a woman, Babylon the great, seated on a scarlet beast and drunk with the blood of the saints, a city of wealth, luxury, and spiritual adultery that had made all nations drink of her fornication. Her fall was announced with a mighty voice — Babylon is fallen, is fallen — and merchants, kings, and seafarers lamented her burning in a single hour, while heaven rejoiced because God had avenged the blood of his servants upon her. God's people were called to come out of her, lest they share in her sins and receive of her plagues, for her sins had reached unto heaven and her judgment would be sudden and complete.
Fulfillment: Babylon's identity is debated — Rome, a future rebuilt city, or a symbol of the world system opposed to God — and interpreters differ over whether her fall is past, future, or both in pattern and climax. The prophecy's moral core is not debated in the text: a persecuting, seducing world power will fall under God's judgment, and God's people must separate from her before that judgment comes. This entry covers Revelation 17-18 as one prophecy of that fall, distinct from the bowl judgments that execute it.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Babylon; Day of the Lord

Prophecy: The Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile of Zedekiah
ProphecySummary: Ezekiel acted out a siege against a clay model of Jerusalem and announced that famine, sword, and pestilence would fall on the city, its people would be scattered, and King Zedekiah would be taken captive to Babylon. The prophecies in chapters 4 to 24 repeat that warning through signs, parables, and direct charges against Jerusalem's idolatry and broken covenant. Zedekiah's attempt to escape by night would fail, and he would be brought blinded before the king of Babylon.
Fulfillment: Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem, and the city fell in 586 BC after famine and assault, as recorded in 2 Kings 25. Zedekiah fled by night, was captured near Jericho, saw his sons killed, and was then blinded and taken in chains to Babylon. The temple was burned, the walls were broken down, and many survivors were carried into exile.
KeyPassages: Ezekiel 4:1-3; Ezekiel 5:1-17; Ezekiel 12:10-14; Ezekiel 17:12-21; Ezekiel 24:1-14; 2 Kings 25:1-7; Jeremiah 52:4-11
RelatedPeople: Zedekiah, King of Judah; King Nebuchadnezzar
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

ProphecySummary: Ezekiel announced that Nebuchadnezzar would besiege Tyre, break down its walls and towers, and plunder its wealth, and that many nations would come against the island city like waves of the sea. The lament over Tyre describes a wealthy trading city, proud of its beauty and wisdom, brought down and mourned by the merchants of the coast. God said Tyre would become a bare rock where fishermen spread their nets.
Fulfillment: Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for thirteen years and reduced its mainland city, and Alexander later captured the island city in 332 BC by building a causeway from the mainland ruins. Those conquests fulfilled the pattern of successive assaults, but the wording about Tyre never being rebuilt is debated, since a city called Tyre still stands on the site today. For that reason this entry is marked Partially Fulfilled rather than as a simple completed prediction.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Tyre

Prophecy: The Flood and the Rainbow Covenant
ProphecySummary: God warned Noah that He would bring a flood to destroy all flesh on the earth, and told him to build an ark so that he, his family, and two of every living creature would be kept alive. After the waters receded, God promised that He would never again destroy all flesh by a flood, and He set the rainbow in the cloud as the sign of that everlasting covenant with Noah and every living creature.
Fulfillment: The flood came exactly as warned, the ark preserved Noah's family and the animals, and the waters receded until dry land appeared. God then made the covenant recorded in Genesis 9, and the rainbow has stood ever since as the sign He appointed. The promise is one of restraint, not of an end to all judgment, and Scripture still points forward to a final judgment by fire.
RelatedEvents: Noah and the Flood

Prophecy: The Fountain Opened for Sin and Uncleanness
ProphecySummary: In that day, Zechariah declared, there shall be a fountain opened to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem for sin and for uncleanness. In the same day God will cut off the names of idols from the land so they are remembered no more, and will cause prophets of falsehood and the unclean spirit to pass out of the land. The cleansing is therefore both inward, washing sin, and outward, ending idolatry and false prophecy in the restored community.
Fulfillment: Christians read this fountain as opened at the cross, where blood and water flowed and cleansing from sin was provided, as John and the epistles describe, and as continuing whenever sinners are washed. Jerusalem has not yet known the complete end of idolatry and false prophecy that Zechariah pictures in the same day, and Jewish tradition reads the full cleansing as still future. The fountain is therefore partly fulfilled: opened in Christ, awaiting its complete cleansing of Jerusalem.
RelatedEvents: Crucifixion; Cleansing of Jerusalem

Prophecy: Four Hundred Years of Affliction and the Exodus
ProphecySummary: In a vision God told Abraham that his offspring would be strangers in a land not theirs, afflicted for four hundred years, and that the nation that afflicted them would be judged. Afterwards, God said, they would come out with great substance, and return to the promised land in the fourth generation, because the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet full.
Fulfillment: Israel sojourned in Egypt, was enslaved, and left at the exodus after the plagues, carrying silver and gold given by the Egyptians, as Exodus 12 records. The four hundred years is a round figure for the sojourn, and Exodus 12:40 gives the longer figure of 430 years, which is why the entry states the promise in its own terms rather than forcing a single arithmetic. The return to Canaan under Joshua completed the movement the prophecy described.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; Conquest of Canaan

ProphecySummary: Paul revealed a mystery: a partial hardening has come upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and then all Israel will be saved, as it is written that the Deliverer will come out of Zion and turn away ungodliness from Jacob. This is God's covenant promise that Israel's present stumbling is neither total nor final, and that the ingathering of the Gentiles and the future salvation of Israel belong together in one redemptive plan. The prophecy looks beyond the present age to a future turning of Israel to her Messiah.
Fulfillment: Fulfillment is debated: some interpreters understand all Israel as ethnic Israel turning to Christ in a future national conversion, others as the elect remnant of Israel gathered through the ages together with believing Gentiles, and others as the whole people of God. What is not debated in the passage is that God has not cast away his people and that their future restoration is promised. The entry is kept distinct from the Valley of Dry Bones entry, which is Ezekiel's vision of national restoration cited with Romans 11:15; Romans 11:25-27 adds Paul's distinct mystery of the Gentile fullness preceding Israel's salvation.
RelatedEvents: Restoration of Israel

Prophecy: Gideon Shall Deliver Israel from Midian
ProphecySummary: While Israel was hiding from Midianite raids, the Angel of the LORD appeared to Gideon and told him that he would save Israel from the hand of Midian, and that the LORD would be with him. Gideon doubted, being the least in his father's house, but the word was repeated with the promise that he would strike the Midianites as one man.
Fulfillment: With only three hundred men, trumpets, and torches, Gideon routed the vast Midianite camp by night, and his forces pursued and captured the Midianite princes Oreb and Zeeb. The oppression that had lasted seven years was broken, and the land had rest for forty years. No human prophet mediates this word in the text, so the speaker is recorded as the Angel of the LORD.
RelatedEvents: Gideon's Victory over Midian

Prophecy: God's Name Great Among the Nations
ProphecySummary: Malachi charged the priests with offering polluted bread and blind, lame, and sick animals, despising God's name while claiming His table was contemptible. Against that small and careless worship, God declared that from the rising of the sun to its going down His name shall be great among the Gentiles, and in every place incense shall be offered to His name, and a pure offering. The LORD of hosts, Malachi repeats, is a great King, and His name is dreadful among the heathen.
Fulfillment: The worship Malachi pictured, Gentiles honouring God's name in every place with a pure offering, began as the Gospel spread beyond Israel and Gentile churches worshipped God across the Roman world and beyond. Christians have read the pure offering as fulfilled in the worship and sacrifice of praise offered through Christ, while the universal honouring of God's name in every place is still unfolding and not yet complete. The entry is therefore partly fulfilled, begun in the Gentile mission and awaiting its fullness.
RelatedEvents: Gentile Mission; Return from Exile

ProphecySummary: Ezekiel pictured a future coalition led by Gog of Magog, with Meshech, Tubal, Persia, Ethiopia, Libya, and other allies, invading a restored and unwalled Israel. God said he would turn Gog back, defeat the invaders on the mountains of Israel, and use the victory to show his holiness to the nations. The aftermath includes the burial of the dead and the burning of weapons over a long period.
Fulfillment: No event in recorded history matches this invasion in all its details, and interpreters place it at different points, including before or after a millennial period or as a symbolic picture of final opposition to God. Revelation 20 uses the names Gog and Magog for a final rebellion, which some readers connect with Ezekiel and others treat as a separate use of the same imagery. Because its timing and referent are debated, this entry is marked Debated.
RelatedEvents: Battle of Gog and Magog
Places: Magog; Meshech; Tubal; Persia; Ethiopia; Libya

ProphecySummary: John saw a great white throne and him who sat on it, from whose face earth and heaven fled away, and the dead, small and great, standing before God as books were opened, including the book of life, and each was judged according to their works. Death and hell delivered up their dead, and death and hell themselves were cast into the lake of fire, which is the second death, and whosoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire. This is the final, universal judgment in which no one is overlooked and the distinction between the saved and the lost is made eternally plain.
Fulfillment: This judgment is presented as future to John's vision and has not yet occurred in the form described, with the books opened and the lake of fire as the second death. The entry is kept distinct from the covered Resurrection and Final Judgment entry, which gathers Daniel 12:1-3 with John 5:28-29 and Matthew 13:43 as the general resurrection and judgment; Revelation 20:11-15 adds the specific throne scene, the books, the surrender of death and hell, and the second death, which the Daniel entry does not contain. Its referent is the same final judgment, but its content is a distinct Revelation scene.
RelatedEvents: Final Judgment; Resurrection of the Dead

ProphecySummary: When Hananiah the prophet broke Jeremiah's wooden yoke and promised that Babylon's yoke would be broken within two years, Jeremiah answered that Hananiah had made the people trust in a lie, and that the LORD would remove him from the face of the earth within that same year. It was a direct test of a false prophecy, with a dated, verifiable outcome. This entry is small, but it meets the test of a named individual's fate treated by Scripture itself as prophetic.
Fulfillment: Hananiah died in the seventh month of that same year, exactly as Jeremiah had said, as Jeremiah 28:17 records. The false promise of a swift end to Babylon's yoke did not come to pass, and the true prophet's word was vindicated within months. The prophecy was therefore fulfilled in Scripture's own record.
RelatedPeople: Jeremiah; Hananiah, the False Prophet; Zedekiah, King of Judah
RelatedEvents: The Yoke of Babylon

Prophecy: Hazael Shall Be King of Syria
ProphecySummary: When Hazael came from Ben-hadad to ask whether the Syrian king would recover, Elisha told him the king would recover from his sickness, yet the LORD had shown Elisha that Hazael himself would be king over Syria. Elisha then wept as he described the evil Hazael would do to Israel: setting strongholds on fire, killing young men, dashing children, and ripping open pregnant women.
Fulfillment: Hazael returned, smothered Ben-hadad, and reigned in his place, and in the following decades he oppressed Israel and cut off its eastern territories, as 2 Kings records. The commission to anoint Hazael given to Elijah on Horeb lies behind this word, but this entry records Elisha's own dated prediction to Hazael himself, not the earlier commission. The atrocities Elisha wept over were the price Israel paid for its unfaithfulness, and Elisha did not soften them.
RelatedEvents: Hazael's Wars against Israel

ProphecySummary: When Hezekiah was sick unto death, Isaiah first told him to set his house in order, for he would die and not live. After Hezekiah prayed with tears, the word of the LORD came again through Isaiah: Hezekiah would live fifteen more years, and both he and Jerusalem would be delivered from the hand of the king of Assyria. The sign given was the shadow going back ten degrees on the dial of Ahaz.
Fulfillment: Hezekiah recovered, lived on, and Jerusalem was delivered from Sennacherib, as the narrative in Isaiah 38 and 2 Kings 20 records. The fifteen years and the deliverance from Assyria both came to pass within Hezekiah's lifetime. This is a dated, personal prophecy with a recorded fulfilment in Scripture itself.
RelatedPeople: Isaiah; King Hezekiah; Sennacherib, King of Assyria
RelatedEvents: Hezekiah's Illness and Recovery; Hezekiah and Sennacherib's Invasion

ProphecySummary: After Hezekiah showed the Babylonian envoys all his treasures, Isaiah foretold that the days would come when all that was in his house, and all his fathers had laid up, would be carried to Babylon, and nothing would be left. Of Hezekiah's own sons who would issue from him, some would be taken away and become eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon. It is a sober prediction of exile, spoken while Babylon was still a distant power.
Fulfillment: Jerusalem's treasures were carried to Babylon in the conquests of 597 and 586 BC, and young men of royal and noble descent, including Daniel and his companions, were taken to serve in the Babylonian court. The prophecy was therefore fulfilled in the Babylonian exile, in the very terms Isaiah used. It is distinct from Jeremiah's seventy-years entry, which concerns the length of the exile.
RelatedPeople: Isaiah; King Hezekiah; King Nebuchadnezzar; Daniel
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Prophecy: The Highway Home: Return from Exile
ProphecySummary: Isaiah foretold that God would make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert for his people to come home, that he would not forsake them, and that the ransomed of the LORD would return to Zion with singing and everlasting joy. Kings would be nursing fathers and queens nursing mothers to them, and the captives would be released and fed on the way. This entry groups the return and highway oracles of Isaiah 43, 49:8-26, and 51-52 into one distinct prediction of the homecoming itself.
