Fulfillment: Under Cyrus's decree the exiles did return to Jerusalem in waves, rebuild the temple, and re-establish worship, as Ezra and Nehemiah record. Not all exiles returned, and the full singing homecoming with everlasting joy has not yet been seen in full, so the prophecy is partially fulfilled: the historical return began it, and its complete joy awaits the final gathering. It is distinct from the Light to the Gentiles entry, which cites only Isaiah 49:6.
RelatedEvents: Return from Exile; Rebuilding of the Temple

ProphecySummary: God told Hosea to name his children as living signs of judgment: Jezreel, for the bloodshed at Jezreel; Lo-ruhamah, meaning no mercy; and Lo-ammi, meaning not my people. Each name announced that Israel's unfaithfulness would bring an end to mercy and to its standing as God's people for a time. Yet the same passage promised a reversal, when those called not my people would again be called children of the living God.
Fulfillment: The house of Jehu ended in bloodshed, and the northern kingdom fell to Assyria, with Samaria captured in 722 BC and its people carried into exile, matching the loss of mercy and peoplehood the names foretold. The reversal was also begun in Scripture itself, when Hosea 1:10-11 and 2:23 promised restoration, and the New Testament applies that reversal to those gathered in Christ. Because the gathering is still unfolding, the prophecy is best read as partly fulfilled rather than finished.
RelatedPeople: Hosea; Gomer; Jezreel; Lo-ruhamah; Lo-ammi; Jehu, King of Israel
RelatedEvents: Fall of Samaria; Fall of Samaria

ProphecySummary: After Ahab had Naboth murdered to take his vineyard, Elijah met him there and declared that the LORD would bring evil upon Ahab, cut off his house, and make it like the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha. Dogs would lick Ahab's blood where they had licked Naboth's, and dogs would eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel.
Fulfillment: Ahab died of his wound at Ramoth-gilead, and dogs licked his blood at the pool of Samaria as his chariot was washed, while his sons were killed and his house wiped out under Jehu. Jezebel was thrown from a window at Jezreel and eaten by dogs, so that only her skull, feet, and palms remained. Ahab's temporary humbling delayed part of the judgment to his son's days, but the house itself was not spared.
RelatedPeople: Elijah; King Ahab; Jezebel; Naboth; Jehu, King of Israel
RelatedEvents: Naboth's Vineyard; Jehu's Revolution

Prophecy: The House of Eli Cut Off
ProphecySummary: A man of God came to Eli the priest and charged him with honouring his wicked sons above God, then declared that the LORD would cut off the strength of Eli's house so that no old man would remain in it. Eli's two sons would die on the same day as a sign, a faithful priest would be raised up instead, and Eli's surviving descendants would come begging for a piece of silver and a morsel of bread.
Fulfillment: Hophni and Phinehas died on the same day at Aphek, the ark was captured, and Eli himself died on hearing the news. Generations later Solomon removed Abiathar, the last priest of Eli's line, from the priesthood and put Zadok in his place, fulfilling the word about the faithful priest. The man of God is unnamed in the text, so the speaker is recorded as such rather than given an invented name.
RelatedPeople: Eli; Hophni; Phinehas; Samuel; Abiathar, Son of Ahimelech; Zadok, Son of Ahitub; King Solomon
RelatedEvents: Capture of the Ark; Solomon's Accession

Prophecy: The House of Jeroboam Cut Off and Israel Exiled
ProphecySummary: When Jeroboam's wife came in disguise to ask about her sick son, the now-blind Ahijah told her that the LORD would raise up a king who would cut off the house of Jeroboam, and that Israel would be uprooted from the good land and scattered beyond the Euphrates. The sign would be immediate and terrible: the child would die as soon as his mother entered the city, and all Israel would mourn for him alone, because some good was found in him.
Fulfillment: The child Abijah died as Ahijah said, and Baasha later struck down the whole house of Jeroboam, leaving none that breathed, as the word had said. The exile foretold in the same oracle came generations later, when Assyria carried Israel away and Samaria fell, and 2 Kings ties that fall to the sins of Jeroboam. One prophecy thus carried both a near judgment on a dynasty and a distant judgment on a nation.
RelatedEvents: Fall of the House of Jeroboam; Fall of Samaria

Prophecy: Huldah: Disaster Delayed Until After Josiah
ProphecySummary: When the Book of the Law was found in the temple, King Josiah sent to inquire of the LORD, and the prophetess Huldah answered that evil would indeed come on Jerusalem and its people for all their idolatry, and the LORD's wrath would not be quenched. But because Josiah's heart was tender and he humbled himself, the disaster would not come in Josiah's days, and he would be gathered to his fathers in peace, his eyes not seeing the evil.
Fulfillment: Josiah died at Megiddo in battle against Pharaoh Neco, before Jerusalem fell, so he did not live to see the Babylonian destruction that came a generation later. His death in battle sits in tension with the words gathered in peace, which are best read as peace from seeing the coming judgment rather than a peaceful manner of death, and this entry is therefore marked Partially Fulfilled. The core of the prophecy held exactly: the disaster was delayed past Josiah's reign and fell on Jerusalem afterwards.
RelatedPeople: Huldah, Prophetess; King Josiah; Hilkiah, High Priest; Necho, King of Egypt
RelatedEvents: Josiah's Reforms; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

ProphecySummary: Near the end of his life Isaac blessed Jacob, whom he believed to be Esau, with the dew of heaven, the fatness of the earth, dominion over his brothers, and the promise that those who cursed him would be cursed. When Esau came in, Isaac blessed him too, but with a lesser portion: he would live by the sword, serve his brother, and in time break his brother's yoke from off his neck.
Fulfillment: Jacob's line became Israel and received the covenant blessing, while Esau's line became Edom and lived as a neighbouring warrior people. Edom served Israel under David and broke away under Joram, matching both halves of the blessing in turn. The blessing could not be taken back once spoken, and Isaac himself confirmed that Jacob would indeed be blessed.
RelatedEvents: Birth of Jacob and Esau; David's Conquests

ProphecySummary: After warning of judgment for idolatry and broken covenant, Hosea promised that God would allure Israel back, speak tenderly to her, and restore her as a bride. The people would return to the LORD and to David their king in the latter days, and God would heal their backsliding and love them freely. This restoration runs through Hosea 2-3, is repeated in Hosea 11, and closes the book in Hosea 14 with healing and fruitfulness.
Fulfillment: A remnant did return from exile and Judah was restored after Babylon, so the return from judgment began in history, though the northern kingdom was never restored as a political nation in the same form. Hosea 3:5 is read in Christian tradition as pointing to return to the LORD through the Davidic king, Jesus, and to a gathering that continues in the Church. The promise is therefore partly fulfilled, with its full and final gathering still to come.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Samaria; Return from Exile

ProphecySummary: Amos warned that Israel's luxurious injustice, false worship, and oppression of the poor would end in exile beyond Damascus. God showed him a plumb line against a crooked wall, and a basket of summer fruit, meaning the end had come for His people Israel. The sanctuaries would be laid waste, the songs of the temple would turn to wailing, and the people would be sifted among the nations, though not utterly destroyed.
Fulfillment: The warning was fulfilled when Assyria deported Israel in waves in 734-732 BC and then captured Samaria in 722 BC, carrying its people to Halah, Habor, Gozan, and the cities of the Medes, as recorded in 2 Kings 17 and in Sargon II's own annals. Amos's promise that Israel would not be utterly destroyed is reflected in the survival of a remnant and in the later return of Judah, even though the northern kingdom itself never returned as a nation. The exile itself is fulfilled; the sifting and preservation continue in the wider story of God's people.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Samaria; Fall of Samaria

ProphecySummary: On his deathbed Jacob called his sons together and told them what would befall them in the last days, blessing each son in turn with a word fitted to his character and his descendants. This entry gathers the tribal blessings other than Judah's, which is already covered by the existing entry on the scepter: Reuben would lose the pre-eminence, Simeon and Levi would be scattered, Joseph would be fruitful and strong, and the remaining tribes each received their own foretold portion.
Fulfillment: The tribal histories broadly followed the words spoken over them: Reuben lost the birthright, which passed to Joseph's sons, and Simeon and Levi received no single tribal territory, with Levi scattered in cities throughout Israel. Joseph's tribes became the strong northern house, and the other tribes settled in the portions their blessings described. Because not every detail can be matched verse by verse to a single dated event, this entry is marked Partially Fulfilled rather than claiming more precision than the histories allow.
RelatedPeople: Jacob; Reuben; Simeon; Levi; Joseph; Benjamin; Dan; Gad; Asher; Naphtali; Issachar; Zebulun
RelatedEvents: Settlement of the Tribes; Conquest of Canaan

ProphecySummary: Jeremiah foretold that Jehoiakim, king of Judah, would receive no royal lamentation and no honourable burial, but would be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn out and cast beyond the gates of Jerusalem. He added that none of Jehoiakim's seed would sit upon the throne of David, and that his dead body would be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night. It is a distinct prediction about Jehoiakim himself, not a repeat of the Coniah oracle.
Fulfillment: Jehoiakim died during Nebuchadnezzar's campaign against Judah, his body was not given a king's burial, and the biblical record pointedly gives him no burial notice of the kind other kings receive, while his son's brief reign ended in exile. The dishonour foretold, rather than a state funeral in Jerusalem, is what the record shows. The prophecy was therefore fulfilled in the manner of his death and burial.
RelatedPeople: Jeremiah; Jehoiakim, King of Judah; King Nebuchadnezzar
RelatedEvents: Babylonian Campaign Against Judah

Prophecy: Jehu's Dynasty to the Fourth Generation
ProphecySummary: After Jehu carried out judgment on the house of Ahab, the LORD told Jehu that because he had done well in executing what was in God's heart against Ahab's house, his sons would sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation. The promise was a reward for obedience in a bloody commission, and it set a precise limit on how long Jehu's line would reign.
Fulfillment: Jehu was followed by his son Jehoahaz, then Jehoash, then Jeroboam the second, and then Zechariah, the fourth generation, after which Shallum struck Zechariah down. The narrator of Kings explicitly notes that this was the fulfilment of the word the LORD had spoken to Jehu. No human prophet is named as mediator of this word in the text, so the speaker is recorded as the LORD.
RelatedPeople: Jehu, King of Israel; Jehoahaz, King of Israel; Jehoash; Jeroboam II; Zechariah; Shallum, King of Israel
RelatedEvents: Jehu's Revolution; Fall of Jehu's Dynasty

ProphecySummary: Zechariah foretold that God will make Jerusalem a cup of trembling to all surrounding peoples and a burdensome stone for all nations, so that all who burden themselves with it will be cut in pieces. When the nations gather against Jerusalem, God will smite their horses with astonishment and their riders with madness, open His eyes upon Judah, and make its governors like a hearth of fire among wood and a torch among sheaves. In that day the LORD will defend the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and the feeble among them will be as David, and the house of David as God, as the angel of the LORD before them.
Fulfillment: Jerusalem survived sieges and attacks in the post-exilic and Maccabean periods, and its attackers repeatedly failed to erase it, so the pattern of a burdensome stone has recurred in history. No single siege has matched the full picture of all nations gathered, every horse smitten, and Jerusalem's inhabitants made as David in one day, and Christian tradition reads the complete defense as belonging to the final Day of the LORD. The entry is therefore partly fulfilled in its recurring pattern, with its complete fulfillment future.
RelatedEvents: Sieges of Jerusalem; Day of the LORD

ProphecySummary: Zechariah's early visions promised that Jerusalem, still in ruins after exile, would be measured, rebuilt, and inhabited without walls because God Himself would be a wall of fire around her. The horns that scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem would be broken by craftsmen, the horsemen reported that the earth was at rest, and God declared He had returned to Jerusalem with mercies and His house would be built there. Later in the same book the fasts kept in mourning for the destroyed temple would become joy, gladness, and cheerful feasts, and many peoples would come to seek the LORD in Jerusalem.
Fulfillment: Jerusalem was rebuilt under Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, with temple and walls restored, so the measuring and rebuilding began in the return from exile. The promise of a city without walls, with God as its wall of fire and nations streaming to it, goes beyond the small post-exilic town and is read by Christians as pointing to the Church and to the New Jerusalem. The restoration is therefore partly fulfilled, historically begun and eschatologically awaiting completion.
RelatedEvents: Rebuilding of the Temple; Return from Exile; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall

Prophecy: Jerusalem Wiped as a Dish Under Manasseh
ProphecySummary: Because Manasseh did more evil than the Amorites before him, filling Jerusalem with innocent blood and leading Judah into idolatry, the LORD spoke by His servants the prophets that He would bring such evil on Jerusalem and Judah that whoever heard of it would be stunned. He would wipe Jerusalem as a man wipes a dish, wiping it and turning it upside down, and deliver the remnant into the hand of their enemies.
Fulfillment: Jerusalem fell to Nebuchadnezzar in 586 BC, the temple was burned, the walls broken down, and the people were carried into exile, with only the poorest left in the land. The vivid dish image matched the completeness of the emptying: the city was not merely damaged but turned over and left bare. The prophets are unnamed in the text, so no individual name is invented for them here.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Prophecy: Jerusalem's Destruction and the Mountain of the LORD Exalted
ProphecySummary: Micah charged Jerusalem's rulers, priests, and prophets with judging for reward, teaching for hire, and divining for money, while claiming the LORD was among them. Because of them, he declared, Zion shall be plowed as a field, Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of the forest. In the last days, the same mountain will be reversed in glory: the mountain of the LORD's house shall be established on the top of the mountains, and many nations will stream to it to learn His ways.
Fulfillment: Jerusalem was indeed destroyed by Babylon in 586 BC, its temple burned and its walls broken, fulfilling the plowing and heaps in literal history. The exaltation of the mountain began with the return and the rebuilt temple, and Christians read its fuller meaning in the nations coming to Christ and to the heavenly Jerusalem, which is not yet complete. The destruction is fulfilled and the exaltation is partly fulfilled, so the entry as a whole is Partially Fulfilled.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Return from Exile

ProphecySummary: Jeremiah repeatedly foretold that Jerusalem would be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, that the city would be taken, its houses burned, and King Zedekiah would be carried to Babylon after seeing the Babylonian king face to face. Those who stayed in the city would die by sword, famine, and pestilence, while those who surrendered would live. The warnings of Jerusalem becoming like Shiloh, and of the valley of Tophet, belong to this same judgment, and are folded into this entry rather than duplicated.
Fulfillment: In 586 BC Nebuchadnezzar's army broke through Jerusalem's walls, burned the temple and the city, blinded Zedekiah after killing his sons before his eyes, and carried him in chains to Babylon, as 2 Kings 25 records. The famine, sword, and burning Jeremiah described all came to pass in that siege. The prophecy was therefore fulfilled in full and in detail.
KeyPassages: Jeremiah 21:1-10; Jeremiah 32:28-35; Jeremiah 34:1-7; Jeremiah 37:1-21; Jeremiah 38:1-28; Jeremiah 39:1-10; 2 Kings 25:1-21
RelatedPeople: Jeremiah; Zedekiah, King of Judah; King Nebuchadnezzar
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Prophecy: Jesus Foretells His Death and Resurrection
ProphecySummary: Again and again Jesus told His disciples that He must go to Jerusalem, suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, be killed, and rise again on the third day. He gave the same pattern in private to the Twelve on the road to Jerusalem, naming betrayal, mocking, scourging, and crucifixion. He also spoke of the temple of His body, saying, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.'
Fulfillment: Each detail came to pass in the passion narrative, from betrayal and condemnation to mocking, scourging, crucifixion, and burial. On the third day the tomb was found empty and the risen Jesus appeared to His disciples, as He had said. The predictions are therefore fulfilled in the recorded death and resurrection of Jesus, not merely in a general sense.
KeyPassages: Matthew 16:21; Matthew 17:22-23; Matthew 20:17-19; Mark 8:31; Mark 9:31; Mark 10:33-34; Luke 9:22; Luke 18:31-33; John 2:19-22
RelatedEvents: The Crucifixion; The Resurrection

Prophecy: Joash Shall Strike Syria Only Three Times
ProphecySummary: On his deathbed Elisha told King Joash to shoot an arrow eastward, calling it the arrow of the LORD's deliverance against Syria, and then to strike the ground with arrows. Joash struck only three times and stopped, and Elisha was angry, telling him that if he had struck five or six times he would have consumed Syria, but now he would strike Syria only three times.
Fulfillment: Joash recovered from Ben-hadad's son the cities that Hazael had taken from his father, defeating Syria three times, exactly as Elisha had said. The limited number was Joash's own doing: his half-hearted obedience set the limit on his victories. Elisha died soon after, and the prophecy stood as his last public word to a king.
RelatedPeople: Elisha; Joash, King of Israel; Jehoahaz, King of Israel; Ben-Hadad II, King of Syria
RelatedEvents: Wars against Syria

ProphecySummary: John the Baptist told the crowds that One mightier than he was coming, whose shoes he was not worthy to bear or to unloose. That Coming One would baptise with the Holy Ghost and with fire, holding His fan in His hand to purge His floor. He would gather the wheat into His garner but burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire, a work of both blessing and judgment.
Fulfillment: Jesus, the Coming One John pointed to, baptised His disciples with the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, fulfilling the Spirit side of the promise in Acts. The gathering and the fiery separation of wheat and chaff, however, still await the final judgment John described. The prophecy is therefore partially fulfilled, with Spirit baptism accomplished and judgment still to come.
RelatedEvents: Pentecost

ProphecySummary: In the days of Jeroboam the second, Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher, spoke a word that Israel's borders would be restored from the entering of Hamath to the Sea of the Arabah. The prophecy concerned the territory Israel had lost to Syria, and it was spoken while Israel was still afflicted and without a helper.
Fulfillment: Jeroboam the second did restore the border of Israel from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah, and 2 Kings states that he did so according to the word of the LORD spoken by Jonah. The book of Jonah itself, with its mission to Nineveh, belongs to the Minor Prophets researcher; this entry covers only the border prophecy as recorded in the Kings narrative. The recovery did not last, but the prophecy was fulfilled in Jeroboam's own reign.
RelatedEvents: Jeroboam II's Restoration

ProphecySummary: As a young man Joseph dreamed that his sheaf stood upright while his brothers' sheaves bowed to it, and then that the sun, the moon, and eleven stars bowed down to him. His brothers hated him for the dreams, and even his father rebuked him, asking whether his mother and brothers would indeed come and bow down to him.
Fulfillment: Years later in Egypt, Joseph's brothers came before the governor of the land and bowed with their faces to the earth, first when they came to buy grain and again when they brought Benjamin. Jacob himself came down to Egypt and was reunited with his son, and the family bowed before the brother they had once sold. The dreams were fulfilled in stages, not in a single moment, and Joseph recognised them as God's doing.
RelatedEvents: Joseph and His Brothers; Joseph and His Brothers

ProphecySummary: In a night vision, Joshua the high priest stood before the angel of the LORD in filthy garments, with Satan accusing him, and God rebuked the accuser, removed his iniquity, and clothed him in rich apparel with a fair mitre. God then promised His servant the Branch, a stone with seven eyes on which He would engrave an inscription and remove the iniquity of the land in one day. Years later Zechariah was told to crown Joshua with silver and gold and to proclaim the Branch who would build the temple of the LORD and bear glory as priest upon His throne.
Fulfillment: Joshua did serve as high priest in the restored temple, so the cleansing of the priesthood began in the return, but no single day in Joshua's ministry removed the land's iniquity in the full sense Zechariah describes. Christian tradition reads the Branch, priest upon His throne, as Jesus, who is both Davidic king and high priest and who by one offering took away sin, as Hebrews teaches. The vision is therefore partly fulfilled: begun in Joshua, completed in Christ, with its temple-building still pointing to the Church as God's temple.
RelatedEvents: Rebuilding of the Temple; Return from Exile

Prophecy: Judah and Ephraim Restored and Strengthened
ProphecySummary: Zechariah promised that God will strengthen the house of Judah and save the house of Joseph, bringing them back because He has mercy on them, and they will be as though He had not cast them off. The sons of Zion would be raised against the sons of Greece, Judah would be bent as God's bow and Ephraim as its arrow, and God would whistle for His scattered people, sow them among the peoples, and bring them again from Egypt and Assyria to Gilead and Lebanon. Their children would see it, their hearts would rejoice, and they would walk in the LORD's name.
Fulfillment: The Maccabean victories over Greek rule gave Judah a measure of the strength against Greece that Zechariah pictures, and Jews did return from Egypt, Assyria, and the wider dispersion in the post-exilic centuries. The full reunion of Judah and Ephraim, the northern tribes long lost after 722 BC, has never occurred as a political restoration, and Christians read the gathering as continuing in Christ, who makes one people from Jew and Gentile. The entry is therefore partly fulfilled, with its complete reunion still future.
RelatedEvents: Return from Exile; Maccabean Revolt
Places: Jerusalem; Judah; Egypt; Assyria; Gilead; Lebanon; Greece

Prophecy: Judgment of the Nations in the Valley of Jehoshaphat
ProphecySummary: Joel foretold that God will gather all nations into the Valley of Jehoshaphat, meaning the LORD judges, and enter into judgment with them there. The charge is specific: they scattered God's people, divided His land, and sold His people for gain. The sun and moon will be darkened, the LORD will roar from Zion, and Judah and Jerusalem will be safe while their enemies face judgment.
Fulfillment: No single historical battle has been identified as the complete fulfillment of this gathering, and the passage's cosmic signs and final safety of Jerusalem point beyond ordinary warfare. Partial judgments on Israel's neighbours did occur in the ancient world, but the universal gathering and final verdict Joel describes have not yet taken place in full. The prophecy is therefore future, with its setting in Jerusalem and Zion still awaiting that final day.
RelatedEvents: Day of the LORD; Final Judgment
Places: Jerusalem; Zion; Valley of Jehoshaphat; Tyre; Sidon; Philistia; Egypt; Edom

ProphecySummary: Because Ammon rejoiced over the desecration of the sanctuary and the desolation of Israel, God said Ammon would be handed over to the people of the east. Its capital Rabbah would become a desolate place, and Ammon would no longer be remembered as a nation among the peoples.
Fulfillment: Ammon lost its independence in the Babylonian and Persian periods and was absorbed by surrounding powers, including Arab tribes who settled its territory. By the later ancient period Ammon no longer existed as a distinct nation, and Rabbah continued under other rulers and names.
RelatedEvents: Downfall of Ammon

ProphecySummary: Because Edom took vengeance on Judah and rejoiced over its fall, God said Edom would be made desolate from Teman to Dedan. In the later oracle against Mount Seir, the same judgment is repeated in stronger terms: Edom's land would become a perpetual desolation for its hatred and bloodshed.
Fulfillment: Edom was weakened by Babylonian pressure and displaced by Nabataean Arabs, and its people continued only as Idumeans under later rulers before disappearing as a distinct nation. The old Edomite heartland in the mountains of Seir no longer bears an Edomite kingdom.
RelatedEvents: Downfall of Edom

ProphecySummary: Because Moab said Judah had become like all other nations, God said Moab's frontier cities would be opened to invaders from the east. Moab would be judged, its pride brought low, and its people would know that the LORD had spoken.
Fulfillment: Moab was overrun in the Babylonian period and later absorbed by Arab and Nabataean peoples, losing its independent kingdom. The Moabites ceased to exist as a distinct people in antiquity, while their former territory passed to other rulers.
RelatedEvents: Downfall of Moab

ProphecySummary: Because the Philistines took vengeance on Judah with contempt and an old hatred, God said he would stretch out his hand against them. Their coastal strongholds would be cut off, and the remnant on the seacoast would perish.
Fulfillment: The Philistine cities were battered by Babylonian campaigns and later conquests, including Alexander's capture of Gaza, and Philistine identity faded in the centuries that followed. No Philistine kingdom survived into the later ancient period.
RelatedEvents: Downfall of Philistia

ProphecySummary: God said he would send pestilence and blood into Sidon's streets and execute judgments in her midst. Sidon would then know that he is the LORD, and Israel would no longer suffer a pricking brier from a neighbour that despised her.
Fulfillment: Sidon suffered under Persian punishment after its revolt and later passed under Alexander and successive empires, losing the independent power it held in Ezekiel's day. Its judgment, unlike Tyre's, is stated as punishment and humbling rather than permanent erasure, and that humbling is what the ancient conquests show.
RelatedEvents: Judgment on Sidon

ProphecySummary: Zechariah announced that the word of the LORD would rest on Hadrach and Damascus, and on Hamath, Tyre, and Sidon, even though Tyre had built herself a stronghold and heaped up silver as dust and gold as mire. God would cast out Tyre's power, smite her wealth in the sea, and burn her with fire, and the Philistine cities Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and Ashdod would see it and fear, losing their kings and their pride. The passage ends with a turn to mercy: the blood and abominations would be taken from Philistia's mouth, and a remnant would remain for God in Judah.
Fulfillment: Tyre was besieged and broken by Alexander the Great in 332 BC, after earlier pressure from Assyria and Babylon, and the Philistine cities lost independence under successive empires, matching the judgment pattern Zechariah announced. The remnant promise, that survivors would belong to God, is read as begun in the incorporation of Gentiles into God's people and awaiting completion. The national judgments are fulfilled, with the remnant gathering ongoing, so the entry is partly fulfilled.
RelatedEvents: Siege of Tyre; Conquests of Alexander
Places: Damascus; Hamath; Tyre; Sidon; Ashkelon; Gaza; Ekron; Ashdod; Jerusalem

ProphecySummary: Amos delivered eight short oracles, each beginning for three transgressions and for four, against Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moab, Judah, and Israel. Each nation is charged with a concrete cruelty or covenant breach: threshing Gilead with iron, selling whole communities into slavery, breaking a covenant of brotherhood, ripping open pregnant women, burning a king's bones, and more. The series ends at home, showing that Judah and Israel will be judged by the same righteous standard as their neighbours.
Fulfillment: These nations did in turn face conquest and displacement, above all under Assyria and then Babylon: Damascus fell to Assyria in 732 BC, the Philistine cities and Ammon, Moab, and Edom lost independence in the same imperial waves, Judah fell to Babylon in 586 BC, and Israel fell to Assyria in 722 BC. The pattern of judgment Amos announced therefore unfolded across the eighth to sixth centuries BC, even though not every detail of each oracle can be matched to a single dated campaign. The series is counted as fulfilled in its national judgments.
RelatedPeople: Amos; Jeroboam II; Uzziah, King of Judah
RelatedEvents: Fall of Damascus; Fall of Samaria; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile
Places: Damascus; Gaza; Tyre; Edom; Ammon; Moab; Judah; Israel; Samaria; Jerusalem

ProphecySummary: In the same Day of the LORD, Zephaniah pronounced judgment on Judah's neighbours in turn: the Philistine cities Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, and Ekron would be forsaken and rooted up; Moab and Ammon would become like Sodom and Gomorrah for reproaching God's people; Ethiopia would be slain by the sword; and Assyria, with proud Nineveh rejoicing and saying I am, and there is none beside me, would become a desolation for beasts to lie down in.
Fulfillment: The Philistine cities, Moab, and Ammon lost independence under Babylon and later powers, Ethiopia faced invasion from the north, and Nineveh fell in 612 BC, within a generation of Zephaniah, fulfilling the Assyrian oracle in dated history. The other nations faded as distinct peoples over the following centuries rather than in a single campaign, so the series is fulfilled in its broad national judgments. The pattern matches Zephaniah's claim that no neighbour escapes the Day.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Nineveh; Babylonian Conquests
Places: Gaza; Ashkelon; Ashdod; Ekron; Moab; Ammon; Ethiopia; Assyria; Nineveh

ProphecySummary: Jeremiah foretold that Nebuchadnezzar would rise against Kedar and spoil the men of the east, taking their tents, flocks, and camels, and crying terror on every side. Hazor, the desert kingdom of settled Arabs, would become a dwelling for dragons and a desolation for ever, its people scattered to all winds. It is Jeremiah's own Arabia oracle, distinct from Isaiah's Kedar oracle, which concerns an earlier Assyrian campaign.
Fulfillment: Nebuchadnezzar campaigned against the Arabian tribes, Kedar's flocks and tents were plundered, and the desert kingdoms of the region lost their independence under Babylonian pressure. Hazor as a desert kingdom disappeared from history. The oracle was therefore fulfilled in the Babylonian subjugation of Arabia.
RelatedEvents: Babylonian Campaign Against Arabia

Prophecy: Kedar's Glory Fades Within a Year
ProphecySummary: Isaiah foretold that within one year, as the years of a hireling are counted, all the glory of Kedar would fail, and the residue of the mighty archers of Kedar would be diminished. The oracle against Arabia pictures its villages and flocks exposed to an invader, with its celebrated bowmen reduced to a remnant. It is a dated, specific prediction against the Arabian tribes, distinct from the Dumah burden that precedes it.
Fulfillment: The Arabian tribes, including Kedar, were attacked and subdued in Assyrian campaigns in the years after Isaiah, with Sennacherib and later Ashurbanipal recording campaigns against the Arabs and their queens. Kedar's independence and glory as a desert power faded under Assyrian and then Babylonian pressure. The short timescale and the diminishing of its archers match that pattern of subjugation.
RelatedEvents: Assyrian Campaigns Against Arabia

Prophecy: The King's Dominion to Earth's Ends
ProphecySummary: The psalm prays for a king who will judge the poor with righteousness, deliver the needy, and spare the poor and needy. His dominion is described as reaching from sea to sea and unto the ends of the earth, with all kings falling down before him. His name is to endure for ever, and all nations are to call him blessed.
Fulfillment: Solomon's reign showed only a shadow of this universal dominion, in wisdom and peace but not in rule over all nations. In Christ the dominion is inaugurated, for all authority is given to Him, yet the nations do not yet universally bow to Him. The prophecy is therefore partially fulfilled, awaiting the day when every knee bows and His reign is openly universal.

Prophecy: The Kings of the North and the South
ProphecySummary: Daniel was shown a long succession of Persian kings, the rise of a mighty Greek king whose kingdom would be divided to the four winds, and then detailed wars between the king of the north and the king of the south. The account follows intrigue, marriages, betrayals, and battles with unusual precision, ending with a wilful king who exalts himself above every god. The final section turns from named historical succession to a king whose end comes without human help.
Fulfillment: The Persian and Greek succession and the Seleucid and Ptolemaic wars in Daniel 11:2 to 35 match known history in remarkable detail, including Antiochus IV's persecution. The identity of the wilful king in Daniel 11:36 to 45 is debated, with some readers seeing Antiochus and others a future end-times ruler, so the chapter's closing section is not settled in the same way. This entry is therefore marked Partially Fulfilled.
RelatedEvents: Wars of the Seleucids and Ptolemies; Persecution under Antiochus IV

Prophecy: The Lampstand and the Spirit, and the Temple Completed
ProphecySummary: Zechariah saw a golden lampstand with seven lamps, fed by two olive trees, and was told the word of the LORD to Zerubbabel: not by might, nor by power, but by My Spirit. The great mountain of opposition before Zerubbabel would become a plain, he who laid the foundation would finish the temple, and the two olive trees were the two anointed ones standing by the LORD of the whole earth. The vision assured a discouraged remnant that the work would be finished not by imperial favour or human strength, but by God's Spirit.
Fulfillment: Zerubbabel did finish the Second Temple, dedicated in 516 BC, as Ezra records, fulfilling the completion promise in literal history within Zechariah's own generation. Christians have also read the lampstand and the Spirit as pointing to the Spirit's work in the Church, pictured in Revelation with lampstands and the seven Spirits of God. The temple completion is fulfilled, while the Spirit's work continues, so the entry is marked Fulfilled for its dated temple promise, with its wider Spirit meaning ongoing.
RelatedEvents: Rebuilding of the Temple; Rebuilding of the Temple

Prophecy: The Land Promised to Abraham's Offspring
ProphecySummary: God repeatedly promised Abraham that the land he was walking through, from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates, would be given to his offspring as an everlasting possession. This land promise was distinct from the promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham, and it was renewed to Abraham at Shechem, at Bethel, and in the covenant of Genesis 15 and 17.
Fulfillment: After the exodus and the wilderness years, Israel under Joshua took possession of the land, and Joshua 21 records that not one of the good promises of the LORD failed. The land was later lost through disobedience, exactly as Moses warned in Deuteronomy, which is why the land promise and the curses of exile belong together in Scripture's story.
RelatedEvents: Conquest of Canaan

Prophecy: The Locust Army and the Day of the LORD
ProphecySummary: Joel described a devastating locust invasion, army upon army stripping the land, as a picture and a warning of the coming Day of the LORD. He called priests and people to lament, fast, and return to God with all their hearts, because the day is great and very terrible. The passage holds judgment and mercy together: repentance is urged before the day arrives, and God promises to restore what the locusts have eaten to a repentant people.
Fulfillment: The locust plague itself struck Judah's crops and temple offerings, and later invasions by Assyria and Babylon brought the kind of national devastation Joel pictured, so the near judgment was fulfilled in history. Christians have also read the Day of the LORD in Joel as pointing beyond any single invasion to a final day of judgment, which has not yet arrived. The entry is therefore partly fulfilled: the historical judgments came, while the ultimate Day remains future.
RelatedEvents: Day of the LORD; Assyrian Invasion; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

ProphecySummary: Paul warned the Thessalonians that the Day of the Lord would not come until a rebellion came first and the man of lawlessness was revealed, a figure who opposes God, exalts himself above all that is worshipped, and seats himself in God's temple proclaiming himself to be God. He will come with Satan's power, counterfeit signs and wonders, and deceit for those who refuse the truth. The Lord Jesus will destroy him by the breath of his mouth and the splendour of his coming.
Fulfillment: No fulfillment is claimed as settled history, because the identity and timing of this figure are debated among faithful interpreters: some see a future individual, others a recurring pattern or a historical figure such as an emperor or papal figure, and the restrainer's identity is likewise disputed. What Scripture states clearly is the sequence — rebellion, revelation, and destruction at Christ's coming — and that the mystery of lawlessness was already at work in Paul's day. The entry therefore records the prophecy as stated and leaves its referent open rather than forcing an identification.
RelatedEvents: Day of the Lord; Second Coming

Prophecy: Micaiah: Ahab Shall Fall at Ramoth-gilead
ProphecySummary: When four hundred prophets promised Ahab victory at Ramoth-gilead, Micaiah son of Imlah alone said he had seen Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd, and that the LORD had put a lying spirit in the mouths of Ahab's prophets. He told Ahab plainly that if he returned in peace, the LORD had not spoken by him, and Ahab had him put in prison on bread and water until his return.
Fulfillment: Ahab disguised himself for battle, but a man drew a bow at random and struck him between the joints of his armour, and he died at evening propped up in his chariot. Israel scattered as Micaiah had seen, and Ahab never returned in peace to release him. The account in Chronicles repeats this prophecy and is not counted as a separate entry.
RelatedPeople: Micaiah, Son of Imlah; King Ahab; King Jehoshaphat; Zedekiah, Son of Chenaanah
RelatedEvents: Battle of Ramoth-gilead

ProphecySummary: Jeremiah's long oracle against Moab foretold that its cities would be laid waste, its pride and its god Chemosh would go into captivity, and Moab would be destroyed from being a people because it had magnified itself against the LORD. Its strongholds would fall, its wine would cease, and its people would be carried away, though the oracle ends with a promise that God would bring again the captivity of Moab in the latter days. It is distinct from Isaiah's earlier Moab lament.
Fulfillment: Moab was conquered by Babylon, its cities were devastated, and Moab ceased to exist as a nation, with its people absorbed into surrounding populations. The destruction from being a people and the captivity of Chemosh's worship match that disappearance. The latter-days restoration strand has no clear historical fulfilment identified, so the entry is marked partially fulfilled, with the judgment fulfilled in full.
RelatedEvents: Babylonian Conquest of Moab

ProphecySummary: Isaiah lamented Moab's sudden ruin: in a night Ar and Kir would be laid waste, Moab would wail on its high places, and its fugitives would flee toward Zoar. Its vineyards and fields of Heshbon would languish, its pride would be brought low, and within three years, as a hireling counts them, the glory of Moab would be diminished. The oracle is a sustained lament as well as a prediction, and it is distinct from Jeremiah's later Moab oracle.
Fulfillment: Moab was pressed by Assyria and later by Babylon, its cities were devastated, and Moab ceased to exist as an independent nation, fading from the historical record. The short timescale and the loss of its famed vineyards and pride match the pattern of Moab's decline under the great empires. The oracle was therefore fulfilled in Moab's disappearance as a nation.
RelatedEvents: Assyrian Pressure on Moab; Babylonian Conquest of Moab

Prophecy: The Mountain of the LORD Exalted
ProphecySummary: In the last days the mountain of the LORD's house will be established above the hills, and all nations will stream to it to learn God's ways. Peoples will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruninghooks, and nation will no longer lift up sword against nation. It is a vision of Jerusalem as the centre of God's teaching and of a peace no human treaty has yet produced.
Fulfillment: No age since has seen all nations stream to Zion in this way or war cease altogether, so this prophecy is not yet fulfilled in full. Its hope is echoed in the gathering of the nations to Christ and in the promised new creation, where God's reign brings lasting peace. It therefore stands as a future hope, not as a completed historical event.
RelatedEvents: The Last Days; The Nations Come to Zion

Prophecy: I Know That My Redeemer Liveth
ProphecySummary: Job, in the midst of suffering and loss, declared that his Redeemer lives and that at the last He will stand upon the earth. He said that though his body should be destroyed, yet in his flesh he would see God, and that his eyes would behold Him for himself. This was a personal hope of vindication and life beyond death, spoken long before Israel's fuller revelation of resurrection.
Fulfillment: Scripture later reveals the Redeemer as the risen Christ, the firstfruits of those who sleep, through whom believers also rise. Job's hope is therefore fulfilled in kind in Christ's resurrection, while its full personal completion for Job himself still awaits the general resurrection. The entry is therefore marked as partially fulfilled rather than claiming Job's own rising has already taken place.
RelatedEvents: The Resurrection

ProphecySummary: Nebuchadnezzar dreamed of a great tree cut down and bound with iron and brass, and Daniel explained that the king himself would be driven from men and live like a beast for seven times. The humbling would last until he acknowledged that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men. After that period his reason and kingdom would be restored to him.
Fulfillment: Daniel 4 reports that the dream came true exactly as interpreted, with Nebuchadnezzar driven out, eating grass like oxen, and restored after he lifted his eyes to heaven and praised the Most High. Extra-biblical records do not clearly document this episode, so the entry rests on Scripture's own report of the event. Within the biblical account the prediction and its restoration are presented as complete.
RelatedEvents: Humbling of Nebuchadnezzar

Prophecy: A New Heart and a New Spirit
ProphecySummary: God promised to gather his people from the nations, sprinkle clean water on them, and give them a new heart and a new spirit. He would remove the heart of stone and put his Spirit within them, so that they would walk in his statutes and keep his judgments. The promise joins cleansing, return to the land, and inward renewal in one covenant gift.
Fulfillment: The return from Babylonian exile began the gathering, and the New Testament presents the gift of the Holy Spirit to believers as the inward renewal this promise describes. The full national and spiritual completion of the promise is still debated among interpreters, with some seeing its fulfillment inaugurated at Pentecost and completed in the future. This entry is therefore marked Partially Fulfilled.
RelatedEvents: Return from Exile; Pentecost

Prophecy: The New Temple and the Restored Land
ProphecySummary: In a vision dated to the twenty-fifth year of exile, Ezekiel was shown a measured temple, its courts and gates, the return of God's glory, a river flowing from the temple that brings life wherever it goes, and the division of the land among the tribes. The vision ends with the city named The LORD Is There, and it includes a prince with a portion in the land. Its scale, river, and land divisions go beyond anything built after the exile.
Fulfillment: No temple matching every measurement and land division in Ezekiel 40 to 48 has been built in recorded history, and the second temple built after the exile did not follow this plan. Some readers expect a future literal temple, others read the vision as a symbolic picture of God's restored presence fulfilled in Christ and the church, and still others combine those readings. Because its nature and timing are debated, this entry is marked Debated.
RelatedEvents: Return from Exile; Rebuilding of the Temple

ProphecySummary: After Jonah's own deliverance from the great fish, God sent him a second time to Nineveh with a stark message: yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown. From the king down to the least, the Ninevites believed God, proclaimed a fast, put on sackcloth, and turned from their evil way and violence. The prophecy is therefore both a warning of destruction and an offer of mercy, with the forty days as a window for repentance.
Fulfillment: The immediate destruction did not fall in forty days, because God saw their repentance and relented, as Jonah 3:10 states plainly, so the forty-day timetable was not carried out on that generation. Nineveh did later fall, completely and finally, to the Medes and Babylonians in 612 BC, as Nahum foretold in detail, so the threatened overthrow was delayed by mercy and then executed in history. For that reason this entry is marked Partially Fulfilled: averted in Jonah's day, fulfilled in Nineveh's eventual fall.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Nineveh; Jonah and Nineveh

ProphecySummary: Nahum, whose name means comfort, announced comfort for Judah and doom for Nineveh, the bloody city full of lies and robbery. He pictured chariots raging in the streets, river gates opened, the palace dissolved, and the city plundered of silver and gold without end. The prophet declared there would be no healing of Nineveh's wound, and that all who heard of its fall would clap their hands, for its endless cruelty had touched everyone.
Fulfillment: Nineveh fell in 612 BC after a three-month siege by a coalition of Medes and Babylonians, recorded in the Babylonian Fall of Nineveh Chronicle, and the city was so thoroughly destroyed that it lay as mounds until its rediscovery in the nineteenth century. Nahum's window is secure: he refers to the fall of Thebes in 663 BC as past, and Nineveh was still standing when he wrote, so the fall came within about fifty years of the prophecy. The prophecy is fulfilled.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Nineveh; Fall of Thebes

Prophecy: No Dew nor Rain: Elijah's Drought
ProphecySummary: Elijah the Tishbite stood before King Ahab and declared that, as the LORD God of Israel lived, there would be neither dew nor rain in those years except by his word. The drought was a direct challenge to Baal, who was worshipped as the god of rain, and a judgment on a kingdom that had turned to Baal worship under Ahab and Jezebel.
Fulfillment: The rain stopped, the brook Cherith dried up, and the land suffered famine until Elijah returned in the third year and announced that the LORD would send rain. After the contest on Carmel, a small cloud rose from the sea and a great rain fell, ending the drought exactly as Elijah's word had governed it. The New Testament remembers the drought as lasting three years and six months.
RelatedEvents: Drought under Ahab; Elijah on Mount Carmel

Prophecy: Noah's Blessing and Curse on His Sons
ProphecySummary: When Noah awoke after Ham's dishonour, he pronounced Canaan a servant of servants to his brothers, blessed the God of Shem, and said that God would enlarge Japheth and let him dwell in the tents of Shem. These were not passing angry words but a prophetic word over the future peoples descended from Noah's three sons.
Fulfillment: The Canaanites were in time subdued in the land, and the peoples who remained were put to forced labour under Israel, while the line of Shem carried the covenant promise forward to Abraham and Israel. How far each clause maps to a particular people is debated among scholars, and the curse falls on Canaan by name, not on all of Ham's descendants. The entry is therefore marked Debated, with the broad pattern of Canaanite subjugation and the Shemite covenant line as the clearest fulfilments.
RelatedEvents: Noah and the Flood; Conquest of Canaan

ProphecySummary: After restoring Peter, the risen Jesus told him that when he was old he would stretch forth his hands and another would gird him and carry him where he would not go. John adds that Jesus spoke this signifying by what death Peter should glorify God. The prediction looked beyond Peter's ministry to the manner of his death, not merely to his age.
Fulfillment: The New Testament does not record Peter's death, so its fulfilment rests on early Christian tradition rather than on a scriptural account. That tradition, preserved by early writers, holds that Peter was martyred at Rome under Nero and crucified, as the stretched-out hands suggest. Because the scriptural record is silent and the tradition, though early, is not contemporary proof, this entry is marked Debated rather than Fulfilled.

ProphecySummary: On the night of His arrest Jesus warned Peter that before the cock crowed, Peter would deny Him three times. Peter protested that he would never deny Him, even if he had to die with Him, and the other disciples said the same. Jesus repeated the warning in each Gospel account, making the denial a specific prediction rather than a general warning about weakness.
Fulfillment: That same night Peter denied knowing Jesus three times, first to a servant girl and then to others by the fire in the high priest's courtyard. When the cock crowed, Peter remembered Jesus's words and went out and wept bitterly. The prediction was fulfilled within hours, exactly in the number and the timing Jesus had named.
RelatedEvents: Arrest of Jesus Christ

Prophecy: Pharaoh's Dreams: Seven Years of Plenty and Famine
ProphecySummary: Pharaoh dreamed twice in one night: seven fat cows eaten by seven thin cows, and seven full ears of grain swallowed by seven thin ears. Joseph told Pharaoh that the two dreams were one, that God was showing Pharaoh what He was about to do, and that seven years of great plenty would be followed by seven years of severe famine throughout Egypt and the surrounding lands.
Fulfillment: The seven years of plenty came, Joseph gathered grain in the cities during those years, and then the seven years of famine arrived exactly as interpreted. Egypt had bread because of the stored grain, while peoples from surrounding lands, including Joseph's own family, came to Egypt to buy food. The prediction saved both Egypt and the covenant family, and brought Israel down into Egypt as Genesis 15 had foreseen.
RelatedEvents: Joseph in Egypt; The Famine

ProphecySummary: Jeremiah foretold that waters rising out of the north would overflow Philistia, that fathers would not look back to their children for feebleness of hands, and that the LORD would spoil the Philistines and cut off Tyre and Sidon's remaining help. Gaza would be bald, Ashkelon cut off, and the sword of the LORD would not rest. It is Jeremiah's own Philistia oracle, distinct from Isaiah's earlier Philistia oracle.
Fulfillment: Philistia was overrun by Nebuchadnezzar's armies from the north, its cities Gaza and Ashkelon were devastated, and the Philistines as a distinct people disappeared from history. The northern invasion and the cutting off of its cities match the Babylonian campaigns against the coastal plain. The oracle was therefore fulfilled.
RelatedEvents: Babylonian Conquest of Philistia

ProphecySummary: Philistia rejoiced when the rod that struck it was broken, but Isaiah warned it not to rejoice, for from the serpent's root would come a viper, and its root would be destroyed by famine and the sword. The whole of Philistia would be dissolved, and a smoke would come from the north against it. It is a distinct oracle against Philistia, not merely a part of the Assyrian oracles around it.
Fulfillment: Philistia was repeatedly invaded by Assyria and later by Babylon, its cities were devastated, and the Philistines as a distinct people faded from history. The northern invasion and the destruction foretold match the Assyrian and Babylonian campaigns against the Philistine cities. The oracle was therefore fulfilled in the loss of Philistine independence and identity.
RelatedEvents: Assyrian Campaigns Against Philistia; Babylonian Conquest of Philistia

ProphecySummary: To rulers in Jerusalem who had made a covenant with death, Isaiah announced that the LORD was laying in Zion a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation, and that whoever believes will not make haste. Judgment would be laid to the line and righteousness to the plummet, sweeping away the refuge of lies. The cornerstone is a foundation for trust, set by God himself in Zion.
Fulfillment: The New Testament identifies this cornerstone with Christ: Peter cites Isaiah 28:16 of Jesus as the living stone chosen by God, and Paul describes believers as built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone. The refuge of lies in Jerusalem was swept away in its fall, and the sure foundation stands in Christ. The prophecy is therefore fulfilled.
RelatedEvents: Christ the Cornerstone

ProphecySummary: To each of the seven churches, the risen Christ promised a specific future reward to him that overcomes: to eat of the tree of life in the paradise of God, to escape the hurt of the second death, to receive hidden manna and a white stone with a new name, authority over the nations and the morning star, white raiment and a name confessed before the Father, a pillar in the temple of God with God's name written upon him, and a seat with Christ on his throne. These are conditional promises of future blessing, given as encouragement to churches facing persecution, false teaching, and spiritual decline. Together they foretell the faithful believer's share in Christ's victory, his kingdom, and the new creation.
Fulfillment: These promises are future rewards, not yet fully possessed in the form described — no overcomer yet sits on Christ's throne or eats of the tree of life in the paradise of God in the consummated sense — though believers already taste them by faith. The entry is included as prophecy because each promise foretells a definite future outcome for a definite group, the overcomers, rather than stating general doctrine. Churches that failed to overcome were warned their lampstand could be removed, which underlines that the promises are conditional.
KeyPassages: Revelation 2:7; Revelation 2:11; Revelation 2:17; Revelation 2:26-28; Revelation 3:5; Revelation 3:12; Revelation 3:21
RelatedEvents: Second Coming; New Creation
Places: Ephesus; Smyrna; Pergamos; Thyatira; Sardis; Philadelphia; Laodicea

ProphecySummary: Daniel saw a two-horned ram pushing west, north, and south, and a goat from the west with a notable horn between its eyes that shattered the ram. The goat's great horn was broken, four horns rose in its place, and from one of them came a little horn that grew great, stopped the daily sacrifice, and cast down the sanctuary. Daniel was told the vision concerned the time of the end.
Fulfillment: The angel's own explanation identifies the ram as Medo-Persia and the goat as Greece, whose first king is followed by four kingdoms, matching Alexander's empire and its division. The little horn is widely read as Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who desecrated the temple in the second century BC, while the vision's references to the time of the end lead other readers to see a further end-times figure. Because the historical core is clear but the final referent is debated, this entry is marked Partially Fulfilled.
RelatedEvents: Rise of Greece; Desecration of the Temple by Antiochus IV

ProphecySummary: When the Rechabites refused wine in obedience to their ancestor Jonadab, Jeremiah contrasted their faithfulness with Judah's disobedience and announced God's promise to them: because they had obeyed Jonadab, Jonadab son of Rechab would not want a man to stand before the LORD for ever. It is a small, personal promise to a family, tied to their obedience, and it is included here as a borderline entry because Scripture itself frames it as a divine promise about their future.
Fulfillment: The Rechabites survived the fall of Jerusalem, and later history preserves traces of Rechabite communities, but a continuous, verifiable line standing before the LORD for ever cannot be traced through history to the present day. Because the promise is perpetual in wording while its later history is sparse, this entry is marked Debated rather than claimed as fulfilled in full. The promise stands in the text, with its complete fulfilment left open rather than overstated.
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

ProphecySummary: After picturing a people whose iniquities had separated them from God, Isaiah foretold that the Redeemer would come to Zion, to those who turn from transgression in Jacob, and that God's covenant and Spirit and words would not depart from them or their children. It is a promise of a personal Redeemer who comes to Zion itself, not merely of a general deliverance. The passage is distinct from the Servant entries, which do not cite Isaiah 59.
Fulfillment: The Redeemer came to Zion in Christ, whose coming to Jerusalem and whose work of redemption turned many in Jacob from transgression, and Paul cites this passage in Romans 11:26 of a future turning of Israel. The first coming has fulfilled the Redeemer's arrival, while the full turning of Jacob awaits its completion. The prophecy is therefore partially fulfilled.
RelatedEvents: Christ's Coming to Jerusalem; The Turning of Israel

Prophecy: The Rejected Stone Becomes the Cornerstone
ProphecySummary: The psalm declares that the stone which the builders refused has become the head stone of the corner, and that this is the Lord's doing and marvellous in our eyes. It then cries, 'Blessed be he that cometh in the name of the Lord,' welcoming the coming One into the house of the Lord. The rejected stone and the welcomed King are held together as one work of God.
Fulfillment: Jesus quoted the rejected stone directly against the chief priests and Pharisees, applying it to Himself as the stone they rejected. The apostles repeated it after the resurrection, naming Jesus as the stone set at nought by the builders and become the head of the corner. The welcome cry was also heard at His entry into Jerusalem, when crowds blessed Him who came in the name of the Lord.
KeyPassages: Psalm 118:22-26; Matthew 21:9; Matthew 21:42; Mark 12:10-11; Luke 20:17; Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:7
RelatedBooks: Psalms; Matthew; Mark; Luke; Acts; 1 Peter
RelatedEvents: Triumphal Entry into Jerusalem

ProphecySummary: Beyond the New Covenant and the Righteous Branch, which are already covered, Jeremiah foretold a return: Israel and Judah would come together weeping, seeking the LORD and asking the way to Zion, and God would bring them back to their own land and restore their fortunes. Their cities would be rebuilt, their fields bought again as a sign of hope, and their flocks would pass again under the hand of him that telleth them. The return strand of Jeremiah 50-51 belongs here, not in the Babylon judgment entry.
Fulfillment: Under Cyrus the exiles returned to Jerusalem, rebuilt the temple and the city, bought fields again in the land, and re-established worship, as Ezra and Nehemiah record. Not all exiles returned, and the full gathering of Israel and Judah together has not yet been seen in complete form, so the prophecy is partially fulfilled: the historical return began it, and its complete gathering remains a hope. The passages already covered by the New Covenant and Righteous Branch entries are not repeated here.
KeyPassages: Jeremiah 30:1-24; Jeremiah 32:37-44; Jeremiah 33:7-13; Jeremiah 50:4-5; Jeremiah 50:19-20; Ezra 1:1-11
RelatedEvents: Return from Exile; Rebuilding of Jerusalem

ProphecySummary: To a childless couple of the tribe of Dan, the Angel of the LORD announced that the wife would conceive and bear a son who would be a Nazirite from the womb, with no razor coming on his head. The child, the angel said, would begin to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Philistines, who were then oppressing the land.
Fulfillment: Samson was born, grew under the Nazirite vow, and fought the Philistines alone for twenty years, killing many and breaking their power in single combats. At his death, blinded and bound, he pulled down the temple of Dagon and killed more Philistines in his death than in his life, beginning the deliverance the angel had promised. No human prophet mediates this word in the text, so the speaker is recorded as the Angel of the LORD.
RelatedEvents: Samson and the Philistines

ProphecySummary: After Saul disobeyed at Gilgal, Samuel told him that his kingdom would not continue and that the LORD had sought a man after His own heart to command over Israel. After Saul spared what God had devoted to destruction, Samuel repeated that the LORD had torn the kingdom from Saul and given it to a neighbour better than he, and then Samuel anointed David, the youngest son of Jesse, as king.
Fulfillment: Saul's house did not hold the throne: he died at Gilboa, and after a struggle between his son Ish-bosheth and David, all the tribes came to David at Hebron and anointed him king over Israel. This entry covers the transfer of the kingdom only; the eternal promise of David's throne itself is already covered by the existing entry on the Eternal Throne of David and is not duplicated here.
RelatedPeople: Samuel; King Saul; David; Jesse; Ish-bosheth
RelatedEvents: Anointing of David; David Becomes King

Prophecy: The Sealed Book and the Appointed Days
ProphecySummary: After the vision of resurrection and distress, Daniel was told to shut up the words and seal the book until the time of the end. He heard that the wonders would last for a time, times, and half a time, and he was given two further numbers, one thousand two hundred and ninety days and one thousand three hundred and thirty-five days. Daniel was told to go his way, rest, and stand in his lot at the end of the days.
Fulfillment: These day-counts have been applied to Antiochus IV's desecration, to the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, and to a future tribulation period, with no single interpretation commanding scholarly agreement. The numbers are distinct from the resurrection promise in Daniel 12:1 to 3, which is already covered, and they remain the debated detail of this closing vision. Because their referent and calendar are disputed, this entry is marked Debated.
RelatedEvents: Time of Distress

ProphecySummary: Before the winds of judgment were loosed, John heard the number of those sealed: 144,000, twelve thousand from each of the twelve tribes of Israel, sealed with the seal of the living God upon their foreheads. Later he saw the same company standing with the Lamb on Mount Sion, having his Father's name written in their foreheads, singing a new song that no one else could learn, as firstfruits unto God and to the Lamb, undefiled and without fault before the throne. The sealing marks God's people as his own and preserves them through the judgments that follow.
Fulfillment: The identity of the 144,000 is debated: some read them as a literal future remnant of ethnic Israel, twelve thousand from each tribe, while others read the number and tribes symbolically for the whole redeemed people of God. This entry is kept separate from the seven seals entry because the sealing is not itself a judgment — it is the preservation and identification of God's people between the sixth and seventh seals and again in Revelation 14. No tribal census is claimed here, since the text gives a symbolic roll rather than a historical register.
RelatedEvents: Great Tribulation; Sealing of God's Servants

ProphecySummary: John saw seven angels pour out seven bowls of the wrath of God upon the earth: painful sores on those with the mark of the beast, the sea and rivers turned to blood, scorching heat from the sun, darkness over the beast's kingdom, the drying of the Euphrates to prepare the way for kings from the east, and a great earthquake with hailstones at the seventh bowl, when Babylon the great was remembered before God. The bowls are described as the completion of God's wrath, fuller and more final than the partial judgments of the seals and trumpets. Even then, those afflicted blasphemed God rather than repenting.
Fulfillment: The bowls are presented as future, final judgments culminating in the fall of Babylon and the gathering at Armageddon, and interpreters debate their precise timing and historical referents, as with the seals and trumpets. No bowl is here matched to a specific dated event in history, since the text itself does not name one. The entry is kept distinct from the seals and trumpets because Revelation presents the bowls as a separate, completing series, not a restatement of the earlier ones.
RelatedEvents: Day of the Lord; Fall of Babylon; Battle of Armageddon

ProphecySummary: John saw the Lamb open a sealed scroll, and with each of the first six seals a judgment was loosed upon the earth: conquest, war, famine, death, the cry of martyrs under the altar, and cosmic upheaval that made kings and common people hide from the wrath of the Lamb. Between the sixth and seventh seals, God's servants were sealed for protection before the seventh seal brought silence in heaven for about half an hour. The sequence presents God's judgments unfolding in order, with his people marked out and preserved through them.
Fulfillment: Interpreters debate whether the seals describe events already unfolding through history, a future tribulation period, or both in pattern and climax, and this entry does not settle that timing question. The martyrs' cry and the call for endurance show the seals concern real suffering and real divine justice, not mere symbols with no referent. The sealing of God's servants is treated in its own entry, the Sealed of Israel, so this entry covers the judgment sequence itself.
RelatedEvents: Day of the Lord; Great Tribulation

ProphecySummary: Seven angels were given seven trumpets, and as each sounded a further woe fell: hail and fire mingled with blood upon the earth, a burning mountain cast into the sea, a star called Wormwood poisoning the waters, darkness over a third of sun, moon and stars, locusts from the abyss tormenting the unsealed, and a vast army loosing death upon a third of mankind. An eagle's warning pronounced woe upon the last three trumpets, and at the seventh trumpet loud voices proclaimed that the kingdom of this world had become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ. Even under these judgments, those who remained did not repent of their idolatry and murder, sorcery, immorality and theft.
Fulfillment: As with the seals, the timing and referents of the trumpets are debated — historical, futurist, and symbolic readings all claim support — and this entry records the sequence as given without assigning each trumpet to a dated historical event. The stated purpose is clear in the text: partial, warning judgments calling the world to repentance before the final kingdom is proclaimed. The two witnesses of Revelation 11, who prophesy during the trumpet period, are treated in their own entry.
RelatedEvents: Day of the Lord; Great Tribulation

ProphecySummary: Jeremiah foretold that Judah and the surrounding nations would serve the king of Babylon for seventy years, and that when those seventy years were accomplished, God would punish the king of Babylon and make his land desolate. Writing to the exiles already in Babylon, he repeated that after seventy years were accomplished at Babylon, God would visit them and bring them back to Jerusalem. The number is given twice, in Jeremiah 25 and Jeremiah 29, and this entry groups both passages as one prophecy.
Fulfillment: From Nebuchadnezzar's dominance after 605 BC to Cyrus's decree in 538 BC is a period of about seventy years, and the exiles did return under Cyrus, as Ezra records. Babylon itself was then punished and fell, exactly as the second half of the prediction said. The seventy years were therefore fulfilled in the exile and the return, in the terms Jeremiah gave.
RelatedPeople: Jeremiah; King Nebuchadnezzar; Cyrus the Great
RelatedEvents: Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Return from Exile

Prophecy: A Son Promised to Sarah: Isaac
ProphecySummary: When Abraham and Sarah were far past childbearing age, God promised that Sarah herself would bear a son, that his name would be Isaac, and that God's covenant would be established with him. The promise was given first in Genesis 17 and repeated when the visitors came to Mamre, with the added word that Sarah would have a son at the set time in the next year.
Fulfillment: Sarah conceived and bore Isaac at the set time God had spoken, exactly as Genesis 21 records, and the covenant line continued through Isaac rather than through Ishmael. Ishmael was also blessed and promised twelve princes, but the covenant promise itself was kept through Isaac, just as the prophecy had said.
RelatedEvents: Birth of Isaac

Prophecy: A Son Promised to the Shunammite
ProphecySummary: The Shunammite woman had shown Elisha generous hospitality without asking anything in return, though she and her elderly husband had no child. Elisha told her that about that season, according to the time of life, she would embrace a son, a timed promise that she at first begged him not to deceive her about.
Fulfillment: The woman conceived and bore a son at the season Elisha had said, and the child grew until a later illness took his life and Elisha raised him again. This is a borderline personal prediction, included because it is a precisely timed divine promise delivered by a named prophet, not a general blessing, and because the narrative presents it as a prophetic word. The later raising of the boy is a separate miracle, noted here only to complete the story.
RelatedEvents: Elisha's Ministry

ProphecySummary: In His farewell discourse Jesus promised that the Father would give another Comforter, the Spirit of truth, who would abide with the disciples for ever. He said the Comforter would teach them all things, bring His words to their remembrance, testify of Him, and guide them into all truth. He also said it was expedient for Him to go away, for only then would the Comforter come to them.
Fulfillment: At Pentecost the disciples were filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke in other tongues, and began the public witness Jesus had promised. Peter explained the event as the outpouring foretold by Joel, now given through the risen Christ. The promise is therefore fulfilled at Pentecost, while the Spirit's ongoing guidance of the Church continues from that day.
RelatedEvents: Pentecost

ProphecySummary: The psalm speaks in the voice of a sufferer consumed by zeal for God's house, bearing reproach for God's sake, and hated without a cause. He is given gall for his meat and vinegar to drink in his thirst, as one set apart and afflicted. The portrait is not a single complaint but a pattern of suffering that Scripture later recognises in the Messiah.
Fulfillment: John records that the disciples remembered 'the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up' when Jesus cleansed the temple, and that He was hated without a cause. At the cross soldiers offered Him vinegar in His thirst, matching the psalm's gall and vinegar. These distinct details, fulfilled in separate moments of Jesus's life, mark the psalm as a genuine messianic portrait rather than a restatement of Psalm 22 or Isaiah 53.
RelatedEvents: Temple Cleansing; The Crucifixion

ProphecySummary: Micah promised that God will assemble the remnant of His flock, the lame and the outcast, and make them a strong nation, with the LORD reigning over them in Mount Zion. That remnant will be among the nations like dew from the LORD and like a lion among beasts, no longer dependent on human help. The book closes with God pardoning iniquity, passing by transgression, casting sins into the depths of the sea, and keeping His mercy promised to Abraham and Jacob.
Fulfillment: A remnant returned from Babylon and rebuilt Jerusalem and the temple, so the gathering began in history, and the Church has read the dew and the pardon as describing God's people gathered from every nation through Christ. The remnant has not yet become the unchallenged strong nation in Zion that Micah pictures in full, and the final reign over the gathered flock awaits consummation. The promise is therefore partly fulfilled, begun in return and in Christ, and awaiting completion.
RelatedEvents: Return from Exile; Gathering of the Remnant

ProphecySummary: John saw an angel bind Satan with a great chain and cast him into the bottomless pit for a thousand years, so that he should deceive the nations no more until the thousand years were finished. Souls of those beheaded for the witness of Jesus and who had not worshipped the beast lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years, in what John called the first resurrection, and blessed and holy is he who has part in it, for the second death has no power over them. When the thousand years are expired, Satan will be loosed for a little season, gather Gog and Magog to battle against the camp of the saints and the beloved city, and then be cast into the lake of fire forever.
Fulfillment: The reading of the thousand years is debated: premillennial interpreters take it as a future literal reign of Christ on earth, amillennial interpreters as the present reign of Christ through the church age, and postmillennial interpreters as a future golden age before Christ's return. The text itself is clear that Satan's binding, the saints' reign, his final rebellion, and his eternal judgment are all foretold, even though their timing is disputed. No interpretation is presented here as settled, and the status is therefore Debated.
RelatedEvents: Second Coming; Final Judgment

ProphecySummary: Jesus told the disciples who had followed Him that in the regeneration, when the Son of man sits on the throne of His glory, they also would sit upon twelve thrones. There they would judge the twelve tribes of Israel, sharing in the rule of the coming kingdom. At the Last Supper He repeated the promise, appointing them a kingdom as His Father had appointed Him one.
Fulfillment: No passage in Scripture records the Twelve already sitting on these thrones judging Israel, and the setting Jesus names is the regeneration, a future renewal. The promise is therefore not yet fulfilled in the present age, though the apostles' foundational role in the Church points toward it. It is marked Future, with its full fulfilment awaiting Christ's coming kingdom.

Prophecy: Two Nations: The Elder Shall Serve the Younger
ProphecySummary: When Rebekah asked the LORD about the twins struggling within her, He told her that two nations were in her womb, two peoples would be separated, and the elder would serve the younger. The word was given before either child had done good or evil, and it set the course of the two peoples who would come from Jacob and Esau.
Fulfillment: Jacob became Israel and Esau became Edom, and under David Edom was made subject to Israel, with garrisons placed throughout the land. Edom later revolted and broke the yoke in the days of King Joram, just as Isaac's later blessing had also foreseen. Paul cites the oracle in Romans 9 as a word of God's sovereign choice, not of human merit.
RelatedEvents: Birth of Jacob and Esau; David's Conquests

Prophecy: Two Sticks: One Nation Under One King
ProphecySummary: Ezekiel was told to write Judah on one stick and Joseph and Ephraim on another, then join them into one stick in his hand. God said he would make the divided houses one nation in the land, with one king over them, and they would no longer be two nations. His servant David would be their king, and they would dwell in the land under an everlasting covenant of peace.
Fulfillment: Exiles from Judah and Israel returned together after Babylon, but the two houses did not become one restored kingdom under a Davidic king in the Old Testament period. Christians read the one-king promise as pointing to Christ, the Son of David, while the complete political reunification of Israel and Judah remains unfulfilled in history. This entry is therefore marked Partially Fulfilled.
RelatedEvents: Return from Exile

ProphecySummary: When Ben-hadad of Syria besieged Samaria with thirty-two kings, a prophet told Ahab that the LORD would deliver that great multitude into his hand that very day, and that the young men of the princes of the provinces would lead the victory. A year later, when Syria returned saying Israel's God was a god of the hills, another word promised the same deliverance in the plain, so that Syria would know that the LORD is God.
Fulfillment: Both victories happened as spoken: the young men routed the Syrian camp at Samaria, and at Aphek the Israelites defeated a Syrian army, with a wall falling on twenty-seven thousand who remained.
